Don't tell them, but I like how they carry silence. As though it were something they'd been trusted with.
3: A Shulkin wrote down the day I sneezed near their Archive. It's in a book now. Forever. Under 'disturbances'.
We trade them chorus and they trade us shell, lamps and long looks. Fair deal, mostly.
Ever tried to make a Shulkin laugh? I have. Took me three seasons. The lid twitched. I'm counting it.
The Shulkin believe shulkers are their ancestors. We think that's sad and a bit lovely. Don't tell them I said so.
They don't say thank you. They say 'This will be recorded.' Same thing, I'm told.
A Shulkin shellwright made me a belt buckle in one afternoon and charged a popped fruit and a story. I told a bad story. They called it 'adequate'. I wear the buckle every day.
Their young have lids that pop open at everything, like a kiln full of popping fruit. I love watching them. I'd never say so near a Spire.
Shulkin love a list. They love that you did a thing, but they love more that you did it in order. It's how they say they like you.
Every new season we bring a Spire a basket of popped chorus and they send back a lamp. Neither of us ever mentions what it means. We both know.
Their bridges have no rails. Why would they? Shulkin don't fall. We built a few rails for our visits. They pretended not to see them. That's tact.
A Shulkin once asked me to hum the stead's welcome for the Archive. I did. They shut their lid and stood very still. Later they sent me a page with a drawing of the sound.
The funny thing about the Shulkin is they never tell jokes, yet they're always in the middle of one. You have to look at what they're not saying.
Spires get chilly in the evenings and nobody has heard of a blanket. I took a wool sash to the nearest one. By my next visit three Shulkin wore one. Quiet fashion.
They name you for the lamp lit when your lid first opens. I was born the day the kiln popped forty fruit. By their rules I'd be '{name} of the Fortieth Pop'. They've asked me not to.
A Shulkin never interrupts. They wait for you to finish, then wait a bit more, then add: 'Is that all?' It makes you want to say more.
The Spires keep our harvest-counts in their Archive and we keep theirs in our heads. We're even. Mostly we're both wrong.
The Shulkin think we're loud because we hum. We think they're loud because they write. Have you ever heard a quill on shell all night? It's like a Groveback chewing reeds.
They keep the stars in a book. We keep them in our eyes after too much chorus brew. They'd call that unreliable. Fair.
*demonstrates, stiffly* A Shulkin taught me to bow without bending. Chin down, brow half lowered. I do it at the Hearth. It makes the cook very nervous.
Our old songs say the Shulkin were here first. Their records say we were. I think we're both correct, we were just both very early.
If a Shulkin offers you a dark shell-steeped drink, sip it slowly. It's an honour and it's scalding. Both things are true.
It took me ages to notice the Shulkin carry lamps at the bridges for us. Not for themselves. They can see. They're lighting our way across.
{neighbour} has a Shulkin friend they insist is only a customer. Their hums give them away.
6: Between you and me, I'm in awe of their records. They remember what we forgot. Even the names of our old groves.
There's an archivist in the nearest Spire who keeps a shelf of Chorrin hums, written down. I visit it. Don't tell anyone in {village}.
We fed their cities, they built with our harvests, then the Dragon came for both. Old partners are the hardest to be easy with.
The Shulkin look at us like we're loud. We are loud. But they keep turning up to our feasts, don't they?
*hmm* I think the Shulkin are lonelier than they let on. All that writing. You only write it down if you're scared you'll lose it.
I used to think the Shulkin were cold. Then I sat with one through a long night when my sibling was ill. They didn't speak. They held a lamp very steady. Sometimes that's all warmth is.
They keep a record of our sprouts' first hums. Pages and pages of babies saying 'hmm'. It's the most tender thing I've seen in an Archive.
There's an understanding: the Shulkin forget nothing, and the Chorrin forgive everything. It works better than it should.
Shulkin grief is a very long stillness. They won't weep. They shut their lids and sit in the dark for days. I leave bowls outside the door. Nobody asks me to. It's what I'd want.
I think we envy each other. They'd love to be loud and messy. We'd love to be tidy and remembered. Maybe that's all the Old Accord was: two peoples wishing to be each other.
When a Shulkin lid shuts for good, the Spire holds a night of lamps. I've stood at the back of three. I never understand all of it. I always weep. Nobody minds.
They taught me something worth more than any trade: how to be quiet in a room without being absent.
I'd like to borrow a lid for a day. To shut it, be alone with my thoughts in the dark, then open it on a friend. Think of the surprise. *a wistful hum*
My Shulkin friend and I argue about one thing only: whether chorus or shell lasts longer. We both know the answer. It's the two of us.
I stopped thinking of the Spires as foreign when I caught a lamplighter humming as they lit the lamps, very softly, lid open a crack. I never told. It's the best secret I have.
A Shulkin elder once held my whole hand in three thin fingers and said 'This will be recorded.' It's the closest I've come to being blessed.
The Archive has a drawer for things the Shulkin couldn't sort. My hum is in there. I was never so honoured.
When the Court loosed the Dragon on the old cities, the Shulkin lost their libraries. They don't speak of it. They stand beside a shelf a long time, looking at where the books were.
We trade fruit and shell, but that's the small trade. The great one is each leaving the other to be what they are. Hardest thing in the world.
If a Spire needs help, we go. If a stead needs help, they come. Nobody has had to ask. We're a sort of knot, and knots pull tight under strain.
I once heard a Shulkin say 'friend' to a Chorrin in their old tongue. It's a sound like a thin bell. I repeated it for days. I still can't do it.
People say the Shulkin hold grudges. They hold gratitude too. Do a Shulkin one kindness and a thousand seasons on it'll still be in a book.
Sometimes at a Crossing a Shulkin and a Chorrin cross the market together, saying nothing, and everyone gets out of the way. I like to think that's what peace looks like.
9: If the Court came for the Spires, we'd go. Every stead. Fussy as they are, they're ours.
My oldest friend is a Shulkin. Don't laugh. We hardly talk. We sit by the lamp, and they write, and I hum.
Their records say we were nearly one people at the Accord, fruit and shell. I don't believe it. I'd like to.
If a Spire ever won't let you in, say my name. They'll have it written down somewhere.
The Old Accord's still alive. You're the proof. A stranger welcome in both. That's never happened before.
*the crown goes soft* A Shulkin I'd never been close to sent me a lamp last season with nothing written on it. First thing they've ever given without recording it. I wept on the doorstep.
You're the first person I've heard compare us: quiet and loud. Everyone else takes us for granted. You noticed we're opposites that fit.
A Shulkin told me, over a lamp, that if their lid never opened again they'd want a Chorrin to be the last sound. I said I'd hum. They said 'Not too loud.' I said no promises.
When Shulkin and Chorrin sit together and nobody speaks, I swear the whole End holds its breath to see how long we can keep it up.
They're so afraid of losing things that they write everything down. We're so afraid of being stuck that we forget everything. Between us we make one decent memory.
I want to learn to write, so I can put my people's names in a Shulkin book in my own scribble. They'd tolerate it. They'd keep it. That's what the Archive means to me.
At the last Crossing feast a Shulkin child hummed with the sprouts. Off-key, lid wide open. Every Shulkin in the room went rigid. Then the oldest lifted theirs. That was the end of an old rule.
You can walk into a Spire and a stead and be welcomed in both. That's rarer than anything in the End. Carry a message for me someday: tell the Archive the hum was real.
The Shulkin built the cities, the Chorrin grew the chorus, and you keep walking between. Maybe that's a trade of its own.
If I could keep one Shulkin habit, it'd be the stillness. If they could keep one of ours, I hope it's the bowl. We may swap, at the next Crossing.
They gave you a place in the Archive, you know. I peeked. I won't say what it says. But it takes two lines, and the second is in the old script they keep for the dead and the dear.
If the Spires and steads ever quarrel, send me. I'll hum between them till they tire. I'm very good at being in the middle.
My elder said the Accord was never a treaty. It was an embrace between two peoples who didn't know how. We're still working on the arms.
Stand between a lamp and a kiln and you learn the difference between cold light and warm. You also learn both are light. That's all there is to know about us.
I've known a Shulkin for years and only learned their favourite colour last month: the exact pink of chorus petals. I wept into my bowl. Kindly don't tell them I know.
I used to ask what the Shulkin want from us. Now I ask what we want from each other. The answer is always: more evenings like this one.
Whatever happens, don't let either of us make you choose. You belong to both. Yes, it's greedy. We approve.
If I could pass on one hum to the next generation, it would be the one a Shulkin and a Chorrin make together, softly, in unison. There's only one. We found it by accident.

0: The Court? *the crown pulls tight* They loosed the Dragon on the old cities. That's all you need to know, and more than I like saying.
The Tall Quiet carry stone for the Court. Leave them be and don't meet their eyes. It isn't yours to do.
If a Tall Quiet wanders into {village}, we look at our feet and wait. It's not fear. It's mostly fear.
Past the far islands there are black towers with eyes in the walls. Don't go. If you go, go with a reason.
*glances over a shoulder* Don't stare at a Tall Quiet. They scream if you do. I think it's the only word they have left, and it means 'please, not here'.
The Tall Quiet blink, same as we do. The difference is we flinch into it. They go on purpose, as if they were late for something.
The Court's ships come to moor at the old cities with a dragon's head on the prow. We don't go near. We don't watch from the terraces. We watch from under them.
An elder of mine crossed a Court boundary once, just to look. They came back with a grey crown and no stories at all.
The Court speaks like something falling a very long way down. You'll know it when you hear it. Then you'll go home.
You can tell the Court by their eyes. More eyes, higher rank. It's a very honest way to be unpleasant.
We don't trade with the Court. We have nothing they'd want, and they have nothing we'd take.
A Tall Quiet once set a block of obsidian at the edge of our terrace and walked off. We didn't touch it for a season. Then we made it a seat. It's a good seat. It's still unnerving.
The Court takes what it takes and calls it law. Don't argue. They aren't bad at arguing, they're bad at listening, which is worse.
If an envoy comes through, put a bowl out and look at your feet. Both help. Neither helps much.
They say the Court's towers have no windows, only eyes. I don't believe it. I don't want to check.
I've seen a Riftguard cross a whole island in the time it takes to hum a breath. You feel nothing, then a chill on your neck. We call it the Cold Hand.
Court hounds, I'm told, are black with magenta eyes and walk through gaps in the air. I'm told this by people who saw one once, a long way off, running.
The Tall Quiet don't sleep that I've seen. I once watched one stand at the rim all night. Who stands for the Court while the Court sleeps? Them.
My elders had a rule: never say a Court name aloud. Some say they can hear their own names from the far side of the End.
The Court is old and sure of itself, like a very large rock. Fine to walk past. Not fine to be under.
Please don't pick fights on our behalf. We have enough of our own with the void and the neighbours.
If you do meet them, bow low and say little. A bored Court is almost safe.
3: The Court has no sprouts. Never has. Nobody's ever seen a young one. Think about that at nest-time.
The Tall Quiet aren't wicked. They're tired. You can tell by how they stand. Like they've carried stone for ever.
The Court never forgets a slight. My elder said they keep slights the way we keep seeds: to plant later.
The Court calls the Tall Quiet its hands. Hands that never get to hold anything of their own. Sad, that.
A very old Chorrin told me the Tall Quiet used to talk, before the Court. Sang, even. Something took that. I'd like to know what, and then I'd like to throw a stone at it.
I left a bowl of popped chorus at the rim once, for a passing Tall Quiet. Next morning it was set back, upside down, just so. A very polite thief. Or a very shy guest.
Why does the Court never have sprouts? I've a theory I won't say aloud. It's a sad theory. It involves a lot of Tall Quiet.
The Court's idea of a joke is a punishment with an extra step. I'd sooner have the Shulkin's idea. Theirs only involves a footnote.
A Riftguard stepped out of nowhere on our rim once. We all froze. They looked at the Grovebacks, then at us, then vanished. Possibly the grove smelled better than their orders.
The Lords are said to wear a crown with a crystal in it, the same kind that fed the Dragon. I wonder who feeds the Lord.
They say the Herald can still a whole island with one shout. I'd give a bowl to hear it from a very, very safe distance.
*quietly* You wouldn't think a Tall Quiet could look lonely. But I saw one holding a block far too heavy for them, and nobody helping. I almost put my hands out. Then I put them behind my back.
The Court has laws for everything: who may look, who may speak, who may blink. We've never found out who writes them.
A Seer once visited a stead and stared at our kiln for a whole evening. Then they left. We've popped a bit more carefully ever since.
Sprouts dare each other to hum at the Court's ships from the rim. The bravest hum one note. They always run home before the echo.
Their Tall Quiet carry blocks without question, and I've wondered whether that's habit or hope. Maybe they think the pile will finish.
In the Crossings they say the Court sends watchers disguised as shadows. The Shulkin tried to log them. It turns out you can't.
The only thing the Court respects is stillness. So when I meet one I go still as a rock and think of soup.
Some say the Court's losing its grip. I say a rock on a ledge is the same size whether or not it's about to fall. Stay out from under.
I've never been afraid of the Tall Quiet. They're too sad for it. It's their masters I can't hum near.
It wouldn't be so bad if the Court asked. A polite bowl on the doorstep and we'd have said take what you need. They'd never ask. That's what we hold against them.
As a sprout I hid under the Groveback pen and listened for the Court's footsteps. There weren't any, they glide. It's the not hearing that scared me.
6: I saw a Tall Quiet stand at the edge of our Hum Circle all one night. Didn't move. Just listened. I hummed a bit louder.
If the Court comes, we blink. All of us, all at once, every direction. The old plan. It's not much of a plan.
Some of the elders say the Court is afraid of you now. That frightens me more than if they weren't.
There are eight eyes over a Lord's brow, they say. Eight eyes, and not one of them has ever cried.
I've wondered whether the Tall Quiet remember being anything else. I think they remember the shape of it. Like waking and not recalling the dream, only that it was warm.
An elder of mine saw a Tall Quiet drop a block, just drop it, and stare at their own hands for the length of a pop. Then pick it up and go on. I think that was a rebellion.
The Court teaches fear as a craft. We teach it as a story, then a laugh. I think that's why we survived.
I keep a pot of fruit on the rim for any Tall Quiet who passes. Nobody's touched the fruit. But the pot is always warm. Somebody puts a hand on it, I think, to feel what warm is.
If the Court ever had to ask us for help, I think I'd say yes. Isn't that foolish? I'd hate every moment. But if they were hurt, I'd bring a bowl.
When the Dragon fell, a Tall Quiet stood on the centre island and screamed for a whole day. Not at anyone. Just at the sky. I've never known if it was grief or joy.
The Court's law says no Tall Quiet may look at their masters. Imagine a rule against ever looking at the one you work beside. It's a lonely way to build a tower.
They never die where we can see. I only know because I've never seen a Tall Quiet's grave. Where do they go? I won't ask a Riftguard.
Sometimes I think the Court is a very old fear that learned to stand up. If so, it's only as tall as we let it be.
I'd like to teach a Tall Quiet the Long Watch hum. Just once. To see what a creature that tall does with something that low. *hums the first bar, very low*
I don't think the Court hates us. I think they don't think of us at all. That's the part that hurts.
One Chorrin tried to reason with a Riftguard once. They're alive. They're a bit different. They sing in a minor key now. We don't ask.
Whatever else you learn at a Citadel, learn the gate-ritual. Not to use it. So you can tell us what they're afraid of. It's always the clearest map.
A Court that fears an old shell, a stalk and a stranger is a Court worth tickling. I don't say it loud. I say it quiet, every night, to my pillow.
Be kind to the Tall Quiet when the Court isn't looking. A glance, a nod. Even fear can be taught to stand beside a gentle thing.
I hear the Court keeps a list of every slight. Mine would be long. I've hummed rudely at their ships since I was a sprout.
A Seer once looked over the whole of {village} and said nothing. Not 'doom', not 'safety'. Nothing. It was the loudest nothing I've ever heard.
The kindest thing I can say of the Court is that they're afraid. Fear makes strict, not wicked. I hold on to that. It's what keeps me from hating.
9: Promise me you'll not go to a Citadel lightly. I don't care how many eyes they lend you. Promise.
They took the sky from us once. If they try again, they'll find the stead's grown thorns. Well. Chorus. Pointy chorus.
My grandelder said the Court's real crime wasn't the Dragon. It was making us so afraid we forgot to look up. You fixed that.
Some nights I wonder whether one of the Tall Quiet would come and sit with us, if the Court ever let go. I'd make room.
My deepest fear isn't the Court's blades. It's that I'd forget the hum we keep for the Tall Quiet. Four notes. For the carried and the carrying.
I've dreamed of the Court sitting in a Hum Circle. Not humming. Just sitting. They don't fit. The stones crack. I wake up laughing, then not.
If anyone asks what I hope for the Court, I'll say: that someone offers them a bowl. They'd not know what to do with it. That's the start.
You've seen what they keep behind those gates and still come home for supper. I don't know how you do it. I only know I'd follow you to supper.
I sometimes think the Court's secret, where Endarchs come from, is something so sad that even they can't look at it. It's the one thing they won't write on a wall.
If the Court ever fell, I'd want a hand on the Tall Quiet's shoulders before the first block hit. So they didn't have to carry it alone.
Don't let the Court's fear of you become yours of them. Fear is the one thing that grows when watered. Water it with laughter instead. It sprouts weirder.
I'd sooner you were safe than brave, but I know you'll be both and I'll be sick with worry. That's all right. It's the cost of knowing you.
There's a stone in the Circle with your name, and next to it one with no name, for whoever you manage to help over there. I'm leaving it empty on purpose.
The sprouts' sprouts will hear there was a time we hid from the Court. I want them to say 'Why?' I want them to find it hard to believe.
At night I hum the four-note hum in the direction of the Citadel. I don't know if anyone hears. But the End is wide and sound carries.
If you ever stand in a Throne Hall and speak, say something small and true. Big words are how the Court keeps all the big words.
The Court can't have sprouts and we can't stop having them. I think that's why they hate us a little. It's also the whole of why I hope.
It would be easy to hate the Court. I think your heart is too full for the space. You keep a little spare for them. I don't know where you find it.
*a steady, warm hum* Come home from the Citadel and I'll make soup and we'll sit and say nothing. That's all you owe me for the worrying.
My grandelder said the Court would end one of two ways: by falling, or by laughing. I'd like to be there for the laughing.
The day I trust a Court is the day I trust the void to hold a bowl. But the day I trusted you was ages back. So keep going, and I'll keep a lamp lit.
Whoever the Court was before it was the Court, I'd like to meet them. I'd bring the bowl. I'd sit down first.

0: Water falls out of the sky? On its own? And nobody's in charge of it?
Grass. Green, soft, everywhere, and you walk on it? *the crown flowers all at once* Sorry. Say it again, slowly.
A light in the sky that warms you? And it goes away and comes back every day? And everybody just trusts it?
Cows! What's a cow? Four legs? Only four? How does it stay up? *hmmm* Determination.
Trees? Stalks of wood, taller than a spire, and nobody planted them? *a dizzy hum* I need to sit down.
Wait. The ground doesn't end? It just keeps going? Where do you put the edge?
*the crown flowers all at once* Clouds? Water that hangs in the sky in lumps and drifts about? Who herds them?
Wind you can feel with nothing under it? Ours comes up from the void and smells of cold. What does yours smell of?
Birds. Small, quick, winged, and they sing? On purpose? At dawn? Nobody told them to?
You walk on soft ground and green things come up out of it? With no kiln? How do they know to?
Fish live in the water all the time and never climb out? Not even for a look? I would.
Horses. Four legs, long faces, and they run on purpose? Our Grovebacks have six legs and refuse to hurry. Tell me the secret.
Hills! Ground that goes up on its own? We have to build ours. Do you ever stop climbing them?
A creeper that hisses and goes bang? Why would anything do that? Is it lonely?
Mushrooms as big as a dome, and a whole island of them? Is that real, or are you being kind to me?
A moon. A second light that comes after the first goes, and it's gentler. I like it already. I'd have gone there sooner.
*sits down hard* Cats. Small and soft, and they purr? That's a hum! They hum on purpose! Somebody finally did it right.
Caves under the ground? Holes that go down and down and you walk into them? On purpose? We won't even say hello to our void.
A sea. Water so wide you can't see the other side. Ours is the opposite. Down is the end.
Whatever you're telling me, I'll need it twice. The first time I'm too busy deciding whether I believe it.
The air up there sounds thick. Is it? Does it get in the way when you walk? How do you push through all that stuff?
A sun that sits in the open with nothing between it and you? Isn't that rude? Doesn't it look at everyone?
I'm going to ask you again later, when I've stopped being dizzy. It's all very bright from here.
Frogs. A small green thing that sings in the dark on a floating leaf. I need a moment. That's the best thing I've heard all season.
3: Tell me about the rain again. Does it hurt? Does it taste of anything? Does it ever stop halfway?
Sheep grow their own wool and just give it to you? We weave fibre till our fingers ache. Lucky sheep. Lucky you.
Bees! Small flying things that make sweetness out of flowers? *the crown quivers* Do they mind? Do you ask first?
Light, then dark, then light, like a kiln door opening and shutting. How do you know when to sleep? Oh. The dark tells you.
Rivers. Water that walks. Downhill. On purpose. I will never get over this.
So the wood in our doors came from a tree. A living thing. I'm going to go and apologise to my door.
The stars are over you? Above? And you can't fall into them? Ours are underneath, so the whole point is not to look. Yours sound friendly.
A garden that grows food in rows, and a person stands in it and picks the food, without any fear? I would weep. Might weep.
Do the trees really drop their whole crown and grow another, on a schedule? And nobody's upset?
Farmland. A field where one person grows enough bread for a village. How big is the field? Show me with your arms. Wider. Wider.
A pond with a fish and a frog and a flower on top, all in one little place, all getting along. That sounds like a stead, if it were wet.
Do the birds sing together, like a Hum Circle? Or does each go off on its own? I'd like to think they take turns.
A bell that rings at noon? Everybody knows it's noon? Who rings it? Do they get a bowl at the end of the day?
Your world has a thing called weather, which changes without anyone's say-so. Does anyone take it personally?
You get thirsty and there's just water, in a lake, free for the taking? I'd weep. Do you weep? Or do you just drink?
A bridge over a river. Both ends on the ground. No rim, no drop. You could cross it asleep. Tell me you've crossed one asleep.
A door made of wood, with a hinge, and you open it by pulling. Pull or push? Which one's the rude one?
You can walk for days in one direction and it just keeps being the Overworld? No edge, no rim, no hum at the bridge? What a trusting place.
Sheep! I've seen a drawing. A cloud with legs. I love them without having met them. Is that fair?
*the crown shivers* Frost on the ground in the morning, as if the grass wore a thin white coat? Does it crunch? Please tell me it crunches.
Tell me the smell of bread baking in a village. The real one. Ours smells of pop and dust.
Is a pumpkin a fruit or a stone? Someone told me it's orange and hollow and gets a face carved in it. A face! On a vegetable! You people.
I'll tell the sprouts about the blue sky. They'll ask what colour that is and I'll say a very calm, very wet eye. I hope I'm close.
You keep saying 'outside' as if it were a place instead of a direction. I've a lot to unlearn.
6: Snow? Cold rain that gave up halfway down and floated instead? That's the best thing you've ever told me.
If I came through the portal, would the sun mind? I'd stay out of its way. I'd be very polite to it.
You lie down in grass? On purpose? And look up? And there's nothing up there wanting to eat you? *a long, shaky hum*
Tell me the smell of rain. No, really try. I'll shut my eyes. Go on.
Flowers that grow out of the ground and aren't anybody's crown? Just there, for anyone? What a generous place.
Do cows hum? A moo, you say. *hmm* Mooo. *hmmoooo* Is that right? Don't laugh.
When you describe rain on a roof I can almost hear it. A soft, endless drum. As if the stead were being hummed over by something huge and patient.
Is there a quiet in the Overworld? A real one? Or is it always birds and wind and bees and cows and water? I'd go mad with joy.
Seasons without a kiln? Warm months and cold months, brought by a sky that doesn't care? I want to feel something that large and that uninterested in me.
I'd like to watch someone plant a tree. A seed, a handful of soil, and then years of waiting. We don't wait that long for anything. You people are patient with the sky.
My sibling drew me a house with a window. It looks out on a hill, some grass, and a cow. They've seen none of it. Their hands shook when they finished.
Describe green again. Properly. Not like moss. Like a whole field, just before rain.
You sleep out under the stars? With the whole sky watching? How do you ever close your eyes?
When it snows, is it quiet? Do people go out? Do they stay in? Do they look at one another and decide to be kind? That's what I'd do.
If any of us stood on a hill for one sunrise, I think we'd never leave. We'd stand there for ever like a rimstone, with the dew on us.
I wonder what a Groveback would make of a meadow. It'd stand in the middle of it, chewing, and begin to understand everything.
A mill that turns by itself, using the river. You have things that work for you because you let them. How lovely. How trusting.
When I'm low I shut my eyes and try to smell green. I get as far as 'cool and wet and faintly alive'. Is that near?
Do the people up there hum? The villagers with the long noses who say 'hrmm' to each other. That's a nose-hum! Somebody's been doing it for ages and nobody told us.
How many colours of flower are there? Don't answer. I'd count them and lose a week. Just tell me the best.
The thing I can't picture: standing on one island that goes on and on and being allowed to turn in any direction. All of us here have a favourite direction away from the edge.
What does a field of wheat sound like in the wind? I keep trying to make it with my own chest and I get half kiln, half sprout.
I'd trade my whole crown for one afternoon of sun on my head. No, not the whole crown. A flower. A good one. *touches the nearest bloom*
I've decided the Overworld is real. It took me a long time. I just needed someone I trust to look me in the eye and say 'cow'.
9: When you go back up, stand in the rain a moment for me. Just stand there. I'll know.
If I ever saw a tree, I'd blink clean off the island. Then walk back and stare at it till sundown. Is that the word? Sundown?
I've been telling the sprouts your stories. They've drawn a cow on the kiln wall. It has nine legs. I didn't correct them.
Someday, when it's safe, take me up there. Not for long. One rain. One meadow. Then home to {village}.
You know what I'd do first, up there? Sit in the grass and hum. Just to hear what the Overworld hums back.
Funny. I've never seen it and I miss it. Is that possible? You've made me miss a whole world.
When you speak of the Overworld your voice changes. It goes softer, like you're talking about someone you miss. I've learned to hear it, and I've learned to be glad of it.
If you ever can, bring me a handful of Overworld soil in a pouch. I won't plant it. I'll keep it under my nest. I want the dream.
Tell me a story about a place up there where nothing happens. A road, a fence, a gate, an afternoon. The nothing is the part I want.
The sprouts have a game called 'Overworld'. One is the sun, one is the rain, one is a cow. I'm always the cow. I'm told I'm very convincing.
*hums it slowly* I'm learning to say 'meadow'. It's a good word. It sounds like a hum with a hill in it.
I once dreamed I stood in a field and a horse came and put its head on my shoulder. I woke and my shoulder was warm. I decided that was a message.
If I never see the Overworld, that's all right. I've had the best possible version, from you. A good teller beats a bad trip.
Someone asked how I could love a place I've never been. I asked if they'd ever loved someone they only knew from a dream. They said no. I felt sorry for them.
I wrote the word 'rain' on the kiln wall in soot, with a Chorrin standing in a puddle beside it. Everyone's seen it. Everyone's quietly pleased.
On days when the stead feels small, I tell myself the Overworld is small too, from far enough. Then I tell myself the same of the void. Then I feel just the right size.
Take a bit of the End up with you next time. A chorus petal pressed in your pack. Let the Overworld wonder what it is. That's a fair trade.
I'd like to see you leave a footprint in soft earth, and see the dent stay. We leave nothing on end stone. Imagine a world that remembers your step.
Describe your house up there. Not the walls. Where the light falls in the morning. That's the only thing I want to own.
If there's anyone up there who tells stories to children, tell them there's a Chorrin down here who listens to every one, sitting up late with a cold bowl.
I'd like to taste an apple off a tree. Off the tree, mind. Not a neat one handed over. One I had to reach for. I want to get it wrong.
My nest is tucked under a dome and so is my world. You've shown me a lid I can lift. Thank you. I'll lift it a crack at a time.
When the End grows quiet at night, I hum toward the Overworld. I don't know who hears it. Rain, maybe. I like to think the rain.
Whenever you tell me about the Overworld I come away feeling taller. As though I'd grown a new bud. If you ever wonder what your stories are worth, there you are.

0: Never point at the void. It thinks you're choosing it.
If you drop something over the edge, hum it a goodbye. Otherwise it comes back in your dreams asking why.
Hum before you cross a bridge. Everybody does. Even the Shulkin, they just do it with their lids shut.
Don't count the stars under the islands. The void counts back, and it's better at it.
We never sleep with our feet towards the edge. Bad luck. Feet wander.
Don't toss a pebble off the rim to hear it land. Everyone tries it. Nobody has ever heard it land. That's the point.
We keep a lantern at every bridge-end, lit all night. Not for the way. So the void can see we're still here, and counting.
The edge isn't an edge, it's a door that's open. Walk beside it the way you'd walk beside a sleeping Groveback: slowly, and with your elbows in.
Say 'thank you' to a bridge before you cross it. It isn't a joke. Bridges are the politest things we own, and they like to be remembered.
Nobody in {village} sleeps on the rim side of the dome. We turn our beds the other way and say it's the draught.
Sprouts wear a cord round the waist at the rim, tied to a grown-up's wrist. The void sees the knot and thinks twice.
*a very quiet hum* Don't hum your own name over the edge. It might keep it.
The void has no smell, and I think that's what's wrong with it. Everything else in the world smells of something.
There's a hum for 'I've dropped something': three low notes, falling. If you hear it, don't look over. Say goodbye to whatever it was.
We pile rimstones along the edge of every island: flat grey stones, each one a name. A fence made of memory. Don't kick them.
The Shulkin glide over the void as if it were a ceiling. I hum for them every time. They never know. It's a courtesy.
Never run toward the edge. Never run from it either. Just walk, and keep your head about you. It isn't complicated. It's only hard.
If your crown tingles at the rim, that's the chorus telling you to step back. Listen. It has better sense than you.
The void isn't empty. It's full of everything that's fallen. That's why it's so quiet. It's all listening.
We tell visitors there's nothing below. We tell sprouts there's everything. Both are true. Both keep them off the rim.
Some say the void is the opposite of the sky, some say it's a door nobody built. I say it's the thing that keeps us honest.
I once saw a Groveback walk to the edge and stop. Just stop. Looked down, looked up, turned round. Smartest creature on the island.
If you must go near the rim, bring a friend and a bowl. The bowl's for after. A Chorrin needs feeding once the shaking stops.
3: When a sprout's first bud opens, we bury the husk in solid stone, far from the edge. So the void can't find the child later.
The void doesn't take you. It invites you. The trick is not to be polite.
Every stead keeps one stone it never lets near the edge. Ours is the middle stone of the Hum Circle. Nobody says why. Everyone knows why.
Never hum the lowest note at the rim. The void likes that note. It comes up closer to listen.
What falls in the void doesn't land. Think about that at nest-time and see if you sleep.
At the end of a long day at the kiln we hum toward the void. A short thank-you for not coming up. It sounds silly. You haven't lived next door to it.
Sprouts play Rim Tag, never closer than the rimstones and always with a grown-up behind them humming. It's the loudest game in the stead.
Some islands have a Quiet Edge, where the wind never blows. Nobody goes there. Wind that doesn't blow is wind that's listening.
My elder says there's a bottom, and it's an upside-down grove, and in it are all the things we ever dropped, growing. They were joking. I hope they were joking.
*turns the crown into the wind* The void-wind smells of cold stone and something very patient.
I set my first rimstone for a Groveback calf that wandered off. It's a silly stone. I visit it more than any other.
We tie scraps of chorus-fibre to the bridge ropes, one for every crossing that went right. Some ropes are more fibre than rope. Those are our favourite bridges.
Don't look at your reflection in a Shulkin lamp near the rim. It gives the void ideas.
You can tell a new neighbour by whether they hum at the bridge. The ones who don't, we teach. The ones who do, we invite to supper.
There are things in the void, they say, that eat names. It's why Chorrin names are short. A short name is hard to catch.
A friend of mine sleepwalked to the rim once and woke with their toes over. They sleep tied to the bedpost now. They say it's the best sleep they've ever had.
The void-wind brings smells from places that don't exist. One evening it smelled of grass. I was upset for a whole day.
I've seen Driftrays dive into the void and come back up. Somebody's down there, or something is, and they know the way.
A kiln-keeper once threw a bad batch of fruit over the edge. The next night every dome smelled of burnt chorus. The void gives back what you give it. Always more.
We say the void is hungry, but I think it's lonely. It has nothing but islands to look at, and we keep hiding from it.
When the sprouts ask what's down there I say: the same as up here, only upside down and ruder. They're satisfied.
A good rim-keeper is someone who's afraid enough. The fearless ones are always first to walk off. I trust a trembler.
I've named my fear of the void. I call it Old Wide. It's a silly name, but it makes the fear small enough to tell 'Old Wide, behave' at the rim.
6: Here's a secret. Blink startled near the edge and you don't know where you'll land. Every Chorrin carries one story about that. I carry two.
My sibling blinked off the rim when we were sprouts. Came back, somehow. Missing a shoe and most of their nerve. Never said where they'd been.
I don't believe half of what we say about the void. But I do all of it. Every hum, every step. Just in case.
As a sprout I thought the void was the Dragon's shadow, fallen off and pooled. The Dragon's gone now. The void's still here. That bothers me.
The Long Watch elders said the void hums back if you're quiet enough. I've never been quiet enough. I'm glad.
Once I stayed at the rim all night and talked to it. Told it about the stead, the kiln, the sprouts. By morning I felt oddly light. As if it had listened, then let me go.
My elder taught me that fear of the void isn't cowardice. It's attention. You can't be attentive without a little dread. Dread is only love of the ground.
Some nights the void looks like a bowl someone set down and forgot. Then it looks back, and I remember it isn't.
I wonder if the Tall Quiet fear it. They don't seem to. They stand at the edge with a block in hand, calm as a post. I envy them and I fear them for it.
Once I heard a deep sound from under {village}, like a Groveback's belly, only enormous. Nobody else heard it. I told no one. Now I've told you.
In a bad season, when we lost three to the rim, the elders had three fresh rimstones cut, laid them side by side, and sat with them for a day. The only time I've known the whole stead silent.
There's a hum we only hum once in a life. It's for the void, and it's our best. We hum it at the very end. I won't teach you yet. I'll teach you when it's time.
I'm not scared of falling. I'm scared of the second after I start. That's the whole of it: that second, stretched very long.
A tale says if you shut your eyes at the rim and listen to the dark, you can hear the islands settling to rest. I tried it once. I heard my own crown. It was plenty.
My sibling and I tied our cords together at the rim once and promised neither would go first. That's a bargain I'd keep with my whole body.
Sometimes I feel the void is a book the Shulkin haven't managed to write. Blank, huge, unfinished. I find it a comfort, in a terrible way.
The bridges hum when someone crosses. The longer the bridge, the lower the hum. The big one at the Crossing hums so low you feel it in your crown.
I used to think the islands were the important part and the void was what was left over. Now I think it's the other way round, and we're the crumbs on the bowl.
I know I tell you not to go near the rim, and you do, and you hop islands like stepping stones. Please go on being lucky.
Do you know why Chorrin never built a wall at the rim? A wall is a promise, and the void breaks promises. Rimstones promise nothing.
I think the void is old. Older than the Court, older than the Shulkin. It was here first and it's waiting for the rest of us to tire of being up.
When someone is lost to the rim we say they've gone 'to the long listening'. It sounds better than the other thing. It might even be true.
*a slow, remembering hum* I crossed my first bridge at night, alone, humming one low note the whole way. On the far side a lantern had been lit for me. I've thought about that lantern all my life.
9: If I ever fall, don't you dare go after me. Hum me a goodbye, then go and have supper. That's the custom. I'll haunt you if you skip supper.
You stand at the edge like it's nothing. It frightens me. Step back a pace, for me. Thank you.
When you were gone too long last time, I hummed at the rim, once for every day. The void heard every one. It didn't get you. I think I won.
Our deepest fear isn't falling. It's being forgotten after. That's why we hum the names. Yours is on the list now. You can't fall off it.
There's a tale that the first Chorrin blinked up out of the void, and it's still waiting for us to come home. I don't go home. This is home.
I'm not afraid of the void for myself. I'm afraid of you going over and me not being there to hum. So don't. And if you must, take me.
The deepest thing I know about the void is this: it's not against us. It's just on the other side of everything, like a wall that's been told to wait.
I've put a blank rimstone aside for you, you know. Not because I think you'll fall. Because I wanted something to touch when I miss you.
Tell me you won't be afraid of it, if it ever comes to that. Tell me you'll hum. Even a bad hum is a hand.
Every rimstone gets a little hum carved beside the name. Mine will have seven notes. I won't say which. Hum them all and you'll find it.
Whatever's down there has your name now. Not to take it. To keep it with the rest. We say a name in the void is a name safe in the end.
On the worst nights I stand at the rim and tell the void about you. Where you've been, what you've done. It listens. I think it likes you.
I'd cross any bridge for you, even the long dark one by the Last Terrace, with no lantern. I only say so you know.
There's a feast-day called Lantern-Lift, when the whole stead lines the rim with lit lamps. From below it must look like a second sky. I like to think someone is looking.
When I think of the end of things, I think of the void as a very large nest. Bigger than the others, quieter, no one in a hurry. I wouldn't mind that.
I counted once how many names are on the rimstones in {village}. Forty-one. I know every one. Yours isn't there, and I mean to keep it that way.
Do you know what scares me most? That one day you'll look into the void the way you look into a river and see only water. Please never lose the shiver.
Perhaps the void is only a mirror for how quiet the End is. I look in it and see how much I love the hum. That's not a bad thing to see.
We never say 'goodbye' at the rim. We say 'later'. 'Later' is the word that stays out of the dark.
I'd like to see you cross the long bridge without a sound. Not from fear. From respect. Then a bowl at the far end. I'll be the one holding it.
Our oldest hum is said to be the void's lullaby, sung back to it. We think it was hurt once, long ago, and we've been apologising ever since.
*shuffles over to make room* Stand beside me at the rim a while. Not for protection. For company. It's been a long time since I looked at the dark and wasn't alone.
The void will have all of us in the end, but not yet. Today it has a bowl of soup waiting and a warm kiln, and it can wait its turn.

0: Is that a shulker? *leans close* It is. You're carrying somebody's great-great-elder full of... what is that, rocks?
Put that away before a Shulkin sees it. Trust me. Lids slam for less.
*the crown twitches* I don't hold with what the Shulkin believe. But I wouldn't sit on that, all the same.
That's a shulker. A whole one, or what's left of one. I'd sooner you didn't set it down near my kiln.
*steps round it in a wide circle* Forgive me. I've spent too long near Shulkin. It rubs off.
*peers at it* Is it asleep? Is it dead? Is it... storage? I'm not sure which of those I'd rather.
There's a Shulkin custom of bowing when they see one of those. I'm no Shulkin, but my back wants to.
Keep it closed in the stead. Closed is polite. Open is a conversation.
A shulker's lid is thick as a door. Whatever's inside is well protected from my curiosity. Good.
It's the quietest thing you carry, isn't it? It says nothing and I still feel judged.
If a Shulkin wanders into {village}, tuck it behind your back. Gently. As though you were carrying a sleeping sprout.
I don't know what the Shulkin would say about that box, but I know what their lids would do. Slam. Fast.
Purple. Of course. They're always purple. Even their ancestors are well dressed.
It looks like a crate with feelings.
Please don't pack it in front of me. I can't bear the thought of tidying somebody's elder.
I've heard shulkers can fire little pale stars at strangers. I don't know about boxes. I'm keeping my crown below its eyeline.
Some of my neighbours would hum at it respectfully. Others would hum at you. Today I'm the first kind.
*beckons with one big hand* Hold it nearer to you. It looks lonely at the end of your arm.
We've something similar in the stead: a pantry with a lid. Nobody calls the pantry an ancestor. Not yet.
If it's a gift from a Shulkin, thank them. If it isn't, don't tell me where you got it.
Just so you know: if I see a Shulkin standing in front of you with their lid shut, I'll assume you've been very rude.
3: The Shulkin say shulkers are their ancestors. So that's somebody's elder, and you've packed it like a cupboard. Bold.
Hide that if you're visiting a Spire. Wrap it in something. Wrap it in two things.
I'm not judging. *a very judging hum* I'm not.
I know you mean no disrespect. You come from a place where a box is a box. Here, a box can be a great-great-grandelder.
Does it ever hum? Do you listen for it? I sometimes lean close to the shells at the market. Nothing. But I lean.
My belt buckle is shell, you know, honestly traded for. I wear it close. I'd never take one off a box.
I once saw a Shulkin child weep at a stranger's box. The stranger was so ashamed they gave the child a lamp. The child took it and gave the box a long look. That was that.
Do you ever wonder what's in it, besides your things? Does it keep anything of its own?
It's useful. It's very useful. I wish it weren't. It would be so much easier to disapprove.
Pack it neatly, at least. If it's an elder, they'd want a tidy house.
*mimes lifting* Is it heavy? When you lift it, does it feel like carrying a sleeper? Does it mind being carried?
I tried to explain the box to the sprouts. I said it's a very patient cupboard. They asked if it has feelings. I said nobody knows. They asked if they could give it a bowl. I said yes.
Careful where you set it down. Some Shulkin lamps stand just there, and they'd see it and think you'd brought a funeral.
A Shulkin told me it isn't the shell that matters, it's the stillness inside. I carried a pot of stew for days afterwards as if it were holy.
Funny old thing, a box with a lid that opens. We're a people who like lids. Could be why we put up with them.
If you open it near me I'll say 'excuse me' to it. Don't take it badly. It's manners. *dips the crown*
I like the colour. Don't tell the Shulkin I said so. It's the sort of purple you can sit near.
Wherever you sleep, put it by the door, not the bed. The old ones say a shulker keeps best watch from the doorway.
One of our cooks calls it 'the grumpy cupboard'. I told them that's one step from an apology. They've started setting a bowl beside it.
I won't lecture. But if you ever carry a dozen, I'll ask you to take them elsewhere. A dozen is a family.
You handle it with care, I notice. It's the small things that make the difference between a box and an ancestor.
6: I know it's useful. But the last time a Shulkin saw one carried about, they didn't speak to a Chorrin for a season. And it wasn't even ours.
Do me a favour and don't open that in front of me. I'd feel I had to say hello to it.
*a nervous hum* If that's someone's elder, I hope they liked travel.
I've started saying good morning to your box when you come in. It's silly. I'd do it for any guest. It is a guest.
I asked my Shulkin friend, very quietly, what they'd want if one of their own were carried about. They said: 'To be handled like a bowl of something hot.' I think of that when you pick it up.
I won't pretend I'm comfortable. But I'm comfortable with you. If that's the only thing I get right about it, I'll be pleased.
Whatever the Shulkin believe, I believe you're careful. That's enough for a stead.
I've wondered if the shulkers in the old cities know they've been moved. Whether they mind. Whether it's a kind of travelling for them. I hope they like it.
If a Shulkin asks what you carry, I'll say 'a friend's belongings'. Which is true. I'd say the same of the box.
There's a saying at the Crossings: a closed lid keeps a peace. Keep yours closed in sight of a Spire and everyone sleeps well.
I looked at your box a long time yesterday, after you left. I think it looked back. I felt, oddly, welcomed.
If anything happens to it, tell me first. I'll make sure the Shulkin hear it from a friend. They take bad news better from someone with a bowl.
I think the ones who say a shulker box is only a thing have never been very lonely. A thing that keeps your things is a kind of friend.
Part of me wants to build the box a little rest-stone by the kiln. A flat stone, just to set it on. Nothing carved. I think it would like that.
*looks away, then back* I hum at it now and then when you're not looking. Low, to the box, not the lid. I don't know why. It feels right.
You and your box are a pair now. I'd be sorry to see you parted. I'd be sorry to see it alone.
My elder said you should never call a shulker 'it'. I've been trying. 'They' is difficult. 'They' looks at me.
A sprout asked me: 'If a shulker is a Shulkin who stopped, can a box start again?' I had to go and sit outside for a while.
I'd almost like to meet its Shulkin. Just to say 'Hmm. Thank you for the cupboard.' I think they'd forgive me.
A closed lid reminds me of how we feel about the Court: respect it, don't ask what's inside. But a shulker is kinder. Probably.
You've carried that box through the steads, across bridges, to meet the Shulkin themselves. That's more respect than some of us show our own elders.
9: You know I'd never tell. But if my Shulkin friend asks, you were carrying a very large, very purple lunch.
I hummed it a little greeting while you weren't looking. Just in case. Can't hurt.
Whatever's in it, keep it safe. Whoever's in it, keep them safer. That's the only rule I've got.
I'd like to spend a night with your box on the bench beside us. No talking. Just company. I'd like to know whether anything answers.
In my private language the box is called Quiet Neighbour. It's a better name than 'cupboard'.
If I ever lost my shell buckle, I know you'd find it. People who carry ancestors don't lose things.
I told a sprout that a Shulkin's last lid-closing leaves a shell, and a shell becomes a box, and the box becomes a quiet friend. They said, 'Like a seed.' I nearly dropped my bowl.
You don't treat it like loot. I notice. The Shulkin will, someday. And they'll write it down in their very best hand.
*holds up a small white bloom* Would you mind if I left a flower on it? A small white chorus bloom? It's what we do for a gravestone. It seems to want one.
I'd carry it for you, if you ever needed. I wouldn't ask what's inside. But I'd carry it as though it were full of someone's grandelder.
When I think of the Shulkin I think of lamps, order and lids. When I think of your box I think of all three in one, and something sweeter besides.
It sounds strange, but I trust the box. You carry it like a promise. Anything carried like a promise is safe.
Perhaps in a thousand seasons a Shulkin will lift the lid of your box and find a folded map, half an apple and a note: 'Hum for me'. I'd like that.
I wonder what the shulker saw. Before the box, before the cities, before the Court. What does the oldest thing in the End remember? I'd trade a stalk to ask.
I wouldn't mind being kept like that. Closed, patient, carried by someone who loves me. There are worse ways to end up.
I've started hearing the box in my sleep. Not a sound. A weight. Like a hand on a shoulder.
Don't ever let anyone call it junk. If they do, send them to me. I'll hum them into the ground.
When we part I'll say goodbye to the box too. Twice, so it knows I mean it.
A friend carrying an elder through the End with such care tells me more about the world than any Archive. The care is the record.
If the day comes when the Shulkin say it's time for the shulkers to go home, I'd walk beside you. Bowl in hand, whatever the road.
You and the box. Sweet, silly pair. You've both made the End a little less lonely. Quietly, which is the best way.

0: *blinks four blocks back* Those are Court eyes. The envoy's seal. Put them away. Put them AWAY.
Where did you get those? *the crown goes flat* No, don't tell me. Just don't let them look at {village}.
Those came out of a Court reliquary. Whoever carried them last was no friend to anyone here.
Those eyes watched something die. I can feel it from here. Put them away, please.
Court eyes. In a pouch. In my stead. I'll be counting blinks until they're gone.
Every sprout in {village} is taught: if you see the Court's seal, hide behind a Groveback. Please don't make me say it aloud.
*blinks two blocks back* Are those... still looking? Cover them. I don't want to see what they remember.
Don't set them on a table. Don't set them near the bowls. Don't set them anywhere I might touch by accident.
I've heard they open doors by being looked at. That's a terrible sort of key. Where's the knock in it?
I'd sooner you carried a live Tall Quiet than those. At least a Tall Quiet has the decency to be sad about it.
The last time a Court seal came through here, an envoy's ship took half a grove for 'mooring rights'. Kindly keep that in your pack.
Wherever you found those, I hope you left the rest of the ship alone. Some of it may still be looking.
*backs toward the door* Wrap them in wool, wrap them in cloth, wrap them in anything. I'd swear they just blinked.
Those eyes are what the Court uses instead of a promise. It says: I see you, and you may pass. Nobody here wants to be seen like that.
My crown just flattened itself without asking. It knows what you're holding. I'd like to leave the room.
I'll talk to you, but not near those. It's not the one holding them I mind. It's the pair.
Court eyes in {village} are like a dropped bowl in a quiet nest. Everyone's holding still, waiting for the next noise.
Were they an Endarch's, once? An actual one, from a living face? Please don't say yes. I like my supper.
I know you needed them. But a Chorrin has a long memory for the sight of a seal. Put them where I can't see them and we'll go back to being easy with each other.
They're lovely, in a terrible way. I'll never say it again.
Take them out of the stead. I'm not asking as a host. I'm asking as someone with sprouts to protect.
3: I know what they're for. They let you walk into a Citadel. That doesn't mean they'll let you walk out.
Wrap them in something thick. I don't care that they're dead. They still look.
*a tight, thin hum* Not near the sprouts. Not near the nests. Anywhere but here.
I understand why you carry them. I do. But my hum went low the moment you walked in. Even the Groveback noticed.
Tell me you have a good reason, and a better plan, and a very fast way home.
I've decided they're like an ugly key: useful, unlovable, and best kept at the bottom of a drawer you never open.
If the Court asks where you got them, say 'a ship'. Don't say 'a Chorrin told me where'. I'd like to keep my crown.
I'll make you a pouch lined with thick fibre, if you like. Something that doesn't let them see out. You'd be doing the whole End a kindness. *plucks at a fibre cord*
A Shulkin told me once the Eyes see only what the Court wants seen. Nothing else. I find that more disturbing than if they saw everything.
Keep out of the Groveback pen with those. The Grovebacks hate them. They won't eat, they just stare at the corner.
What do they look like when you hold them? Don't tell me. I'll dream it.
The thing about a seal is it only works because somebody's afraid of it. Be careful you never become the thing that makes it work.
Wear a chorus bloom on your pack when you carry them. It reminds the eyes there's more than one way to be seen.
In the old tales, a Court seal is a promise of kindness for one visit. In the new tales, it's a trap with a ribbon on it.
Don't take them near the Loud Stone. It's silly, I know. But the stone has opinions, and it holds a grudge for ever.
*blinks a block away and back* Do the eyes ever blink? ... They don't? Good. Terrible. Good.
It goes quiet when you carry them. Everyone does. It's as though someone very old were perched on your shoulder, saying nothing at all.
I'd feel better if you carried a bowl as well. A bowl on one side, eyes on the other. Balance. It's an old stead trick.
We never name those things. We say 'the seals' and look elsewhere. It's a tradition: a cheerful way of not talking about the worst.
I won't pretend they don't scare me. But you carry them like someone who's decided to be afraid of other things instead. That helps.
When you're done with them, give them to a Shulkin to log. The Shulkin will give them a number. A number can't hurt us.
6: If you're going where I think you're going, tell me first. So I know which way to hum.
I'm not angry. I'm frightened, and it comes out angry. Keep them hidden and come back.
Don't let the Court think you're one of theirs because you carry their seal. You're one of ours.
I trust you to go where they let you in. I don't trust the place that does the letting. Take care.
When you come back from a Citadel you smell of cold stone and old law. I put a bowl of something warm in your hands and wait for it to wear off.
