My first firing, I was so frightened I hummed the whole time, and a whole batch popped on the beat. The elder said I'd found the kiln's pulse. I've been listening for it ever since.
I know every kiln-keeper from here to the far islands by the sound of their chimney. Some chimneys sound lonely. I hum back, in case they can hear.
The kiln keeps me up some nights, the way a Groveback keeps a herder up. It isn't the noise. It's wondering if it's all right.
I let a whole night's batch scorch once, because I was staring at the embers and thinking about nothing. The stead ate toasted chorus for a week and called it a feast.
Sometimes I fire a half batch just so the wall is warm for anyone who needs somewhere to lean. People have cried on that wall. I pretend not to see.
There's a brick near the base I never replaced. It's cracked down the middle and holds fine. I like it. It has the look of someone who's been through things.
My hearing isn't what it was, but I've learned to feel the pops through my feet. The island hums them back up. It's like being sung to from underneath.
I'll tell you why I stay at the kiln, though it's silly. Everything else in life hides and waits. The kiln just says what it means, as loud as it can. I envy that.
9: Here. Put your hand on the kiln wall. Feel it hum? That's what home feels like, to me.
I'd like you to pop a batch someday. Your first. We'd ring the stones for you. Everybody gets a ring for their first.
I'll be honest, I'm going deaf. Slowly. Worth it. Every bang was worth it. Don't tell {neighbour}, they'll fuss.
When I'm gone they'll say {name} was the loudest thing in {village}. Correct them. Second loudest. The kiln was first.
I've asked the stonecutter to leave one brick loose in the kiln wall the day I go into the dark. A little gap for the heat to get out. And me, I suppose.
If you ever hear the kiln stop for a whole day, come and find me. I don't stop for a whole day. Not for a feast, not for a fever.
I never thanked you properly. The night after the Dragon fell, I fired the kiln in the open air, smoke and all, and no wing came. I stood in its glow and cried like a sprout.
I want my last batch to be the loudest. The whole stead will hear it and know who's gone. And then they'll eat it. That's the right way round.
I made a little clay cup in the shape of the kiln door and fired it with the last batch of the year. It sits by my nest. It's yours when I'm gone. Or sooner, if you ask.
Every kiln-keeper has a private word for the fire. Mine is 'ready'. I say it before every pop. I've never told anyone that.
When I'm worried I fire the kiln empty, just to hear it rumble. It sounds like a big friend clearing their throat.
Stand right here by me for the next pop. That's it. Feel it in your ribs? Now you know how I hear you when you laugh.
You know why I don't mind going deaf? I've heard the best things already. The kiln, the sprouts, the Dragon's silence, and you saying hello.

0: End stone in, end-stone bricks out. Square, neat, and stronger than they look. Like me.
Cutting stone the same colour as your own arm. Took me a year to stop flinching.
Mind the stacks. They're straight now. They won't be if you knock them.
I cut the bricks for every dome in {village}. If one leaks, it's my fault. None leak.
I measure in hand-spans. Mine are wider than {neighbour}'s, so don't ask me to build them a door. They'd have to go through sideways.
End stone has a grain, like a long slow ripple. Cut along it and it splits clean. Cut across and it flakes at you out of spite.
The quarry is the underside of the island, where the stone is oldest. You hang from a rope and cut upward. Not for anyone who likes their feet on things.
Round doors are the hardest. A square door forgives a bad cut. A round one shows every wobble for as long as it stands.
I cut with a chisel tipped in Shulkin shell. It cost me a season of bricks. It cuts like a thought. I sleep next to it.
Stone dust gets everywhere. My crown, my sash, the stew. The cook says it's seasoning. The cook is trying to be kind.
My cousin is a kiln-keeper and I'm a stonecutter, so between us we're the same stone as the walls. People say we blend in. People are right.
A new dome starts with a peg and a cord. Peg in the middle, cord round it, scratch the circle. Every dome in {village} began that way. Simple things last.
If you want to help, carry a brick and say nothing. That's the finest compliment a stonecutter can pay.
3: Good stone rings when you tap it. Bad stone thuds. Most strangers thud. You ring, a bit.
The Shulkin buy my bricks for their plinths. They inspect every one. Edge, face, edge, face. I wait. I hum. They buy.
I like stone. It doesn't argue, it doesn't sulk, and it keeps its shape.
Got a chip out of my thumb on my first cut. I keep it as a reminder. Of what, I've forgotten.
A brick has a face, a bed and two edges. Lay it on its bed and it carries the whole dome. Lay it on its face and it cracks and sulks. Bricks are particular.
I never cut when I'm angry. The stone feels it and the cut goes wrong. On bad days I stack. The straightest stacks in the End are mine.
The dark flecks in some stone are obsidian, tougher and heavier. Chorrin with dark flecks in their skin make the best stonecutters. Not that I'm biased.
The foundation stone of a dome is laid by the eldest and hummed over by the youngest. That way the dome learns both voices.
A Shulkin once asked me for a brick with a perfect right angle. I gave them one. They measured it and said 'acceptable'. I carved the word on the underside of the next brick.
Sprouts love the offcuts. They stack them into towers, knock them down, and stack them again. That's how the best stonecutters start.
I can read a day by my hands. Aching in the right places, rough in the right places, that's a good one. A bad day, they're just tired.
The Yard is where I work, and anyone may come and watch. Sprouts, elders, once a very confused Shulkin. I like being watched. It keeps the lines straight.
To split a big block, tap along the line, twelve taps, and then a thirteenth, harder. It opens like a seed. Never the twelfth tap. Always the thirteenth.
6: Every dome I've cut for is a family that sleeps safe. That's the part that matters. The bricks are just bricks.
There's a brick in the Hum Circle I cut when I was barely more than a sprout. Crooked. They kept it anyway. I love them for it.
I'm cutting a new step for the kiln-keeper. They don't know yet. They keep tripping on the old one.
Sometimes I hum into a brick before it's laid. Just a little hum. So every dome's got a bit of song in its walls.
Each of us carves a mark on the underside of our first brick, the one nobody will ever see. Mine's a little spiral. I won't say whereabouts. It's mine.
{village} has a row of small stones along its rim, one for every Chorrin who has gone into the dark. I cut the names on every new one. It's the work I mind most, and the work I'd let nobody else do.
I cut stone for ten years before I felt a block open under the chisel, like it had been waiting for me. I've been chasing that feeling ever since.
My back is a map of every dome in {village}. Left shoulder, the Hum Circle. Right hip, the long wall. The rest, mostly the kiln.
I'm slower these days, and the stone has noticed. It lets me cut an easy line while I rest. That's friendship, between a Chorrin and a rock.
What nobody tells you about stone is that it's patient. A wall I cut as a sprout will be standing when the stead has forgotten my name. That's frightening and comforting in the same breath.
I once cut a stone seat for a Shulkin who had never sat down. They glided past it for a whole season, unsure. Then one evening they sat. I wasn't looking. I was told, and I cried.
Hum while you chisel and the line comes out smoother. I don't know why. I've asked the stone. It won't say.
Give me a quiet afternoon and a good block and I'm as happy as a Groveback in the middle of its own shade. I made that up. It's the best I've got.
9: I cut your name into a brick. It's in the wall of the Cook's Hearth, low down where you'd lean. Go and find it.
When I'm too old to lift, I'll sit in the Yard tapping bricks and telling sprouts which ones ring. Seems a good end.
The old cities were built of chorus and stone. The chorus was ours. Some of the stone was ours too. Nobody remembers that bit but me.
If {village} ever needs real walls, walls against the Court, I'll cut them. Every brick. Don't let it come to that.
I've cut a seat for you by the Yard wall. Plain, low, your height as near as I could judge. Nobody else sits there. They've tried and been looked at.
I'm teaching a sprout to hold a chisel. They're hopeless. They're also me, many seasons ago. I find I mind less every day.
When I go into the dark, I want my last stone cut by the sprout I'm teaching, even if it's crooked. Especially if it's crooked.
Once I tried to cut a stone that said 'thank you' and couldn't think what shape it should be. In the end I made it round, like a kiln door. Round means everything in {village}. It's yours someday.
A good wall isn't strong because of its stones. It's strong because of what holds them together. That's you, going from door to door in {village}. Good mortar.
Your hand is soft and mine is stone. Hold them together a moment. There. That's most of what I know about friendship.
Everything I've ever cut, I cut for someone to sit on, lean on or sleep behind. You're the first I've cut for who never asked.
I have never drawn a straight line in my head. They come out of my hands. If you want to know me, don't ask me questions. Watch my hands. They're more honest.
In the Long Watch I cut stone for walls I never dared to lift. Now every block I cut goes into a wall I can see standing in the open. You gave me that. I'm cutting you something in return.

0: Chorus in every dish. Chorus soup, chorus cakes, chorus with chorus on top. Don't ask for anything else, there isn't anything else.
Everyone eats at the Hearth. Everyone. If you're in {village} at supper, you're at the table. Sit.
I don't measure. I hum until it smells right. Then I hum a bit more, for luck.
Popped chorus, a pinch of shell salt, and patience. That's the whole recipe. The patience is the hard bit.
Rule of the Hearth: elders are served first, sprouts second, and the sprouts' bowls are always the fullest. Don't ask. I have a soft spot for sprouts.
Sweet-fried chorus flowers are for feast days only. Any other day they'd be a habit, and I don't cook habits. I cook food.
The pot at the Hearth is older than the Hearth. It was carried here on a back through the Long Watch. I'd sooner lose an arm than the pot.
Shell salt comes from the Shulkin, a pinch at a time in a twist of cloth. I count the pinches. They count the pinches. We both pretend we don't.
A pot of stew wants three things: heat, time, and someone stirring who isn't thinking about something else. The third is the hardest.
Don't scrape the bottom of the pot. The scorched part belongs to the sprouts. It's the law. It was the law before I was born.
Chorus flowers are bitter, chorus fruit is sweet and chorus stalk is tough as a boot. Balance the three and don't speak to me till it's done.
The ladle's name is Steady. It's earned the name. Three cooks before me, and it has never once been dropped.
I cook for the whole stead, which means cooking for everyone's taste at once, which means nobody's. It's the fairest cooking there is.
3: Cooking for a whole stead's like herding Grovebacks. Everyone wants feeding at once and nobody says thank you till after.
You're thin. Overworld thin. Sit. No, sit. Here's a bowl. Here's another bowl.
{neighbour} complains about everything I make, then has three helpings. That's how you know it's good.
Once a trader brought me a potato. One. I made a stew of it for the whole stead. Best day of my life.
When someone's sad I make them a flat-cake and say nothing. When they're glad I make them a flat-cake and say far too much. Same cake, different cook.
We still make the Long Watch cake once a year, cold and dry and hard as a brick. We chew it and remember. Then we have the good stew.
A trader once gave me a cup of milk from an Overworld creature. I held it all evening and couldn't bring myself to drink it. A sprout knocked it over. I forgave them. Slowly.
Shulkin guests sniff the food, taste it, and then very quietly hold out the bowl for more. Never a word. I've learned to read the bowl.
I plan the week's meals on the wall in charcoal, and {neighbour} rubs it out every evening and writes the dish they want. Neither of us has mentioned it.
Fried stalk-shoots are a treat. Hot, salty, gone in a breath. If there's one left over there's a fight, and the fight is the second-best part.
A good cook tastes everything three times. Once to see if it's right, once to be sure, and once because it's good.
The smell reaches the far terrace about now. Watch. Heads will pop up along the rows one by one, like stalks. Every supper, the same show.
I keep a tally on the wall of everyone who's asked for seconds. {neighbour} leads by miles. You're third. You could take second if you tried.
6: The Hearth's open all round on purpose. So nobody eats alone. Not even when they want to.
Bring me something from the Overworld to cook. Anything. I want to know what the rest of the world tastes like.
In the Long Watch we ate cold and quiet by froglight, so the Dragon wouldn't see a fire. Now look. Fire, all night.
I keep a bowl warm at the edge of the oven for whoever's late. Lately it's been you. I don't mind.
I cooked my first meal for the stead when I was barely taller than the table. It was terrible. Everyone ate every bite and called it wonderful. That's why I cook. Not for the food. For that.
There's a dish I make only once a year, on the day my elder went into the dark. Plain chorus, plain pot, no salt. It's the best thing I make, and I make it once a year so nobody tires of it.
I'm teaching a sprout to stir. First lesson: don't stop, and don't spill. Second lesson: spill anyway, and keep going. That's the whole craft.
On nights when the void-wind howls, I make extra and set it by the door. Someone always turns up cold. It's never the one I expect.
I've a pot for sad days and a pot for glad ones, and the funny thing is that the stew is the same. It's the eater who changes.
Do you know what I do when I can't sleep? I get up and chop. Roots, stalks, fruit. By morning I've made enough for two days, and the thinking's done too.
The first time you ate at my Hearth you didn't say a word. You ate every bite and looked at me. I knew then. That's all a cook wants. To be looked at like that.
I wish I could cook you what you ate as a child. Whatever it was. I'd get it wrong, I'm sure. You'd eat it anyway. I'd cry.
A kitchen full of steam is the closest we get to weather. I stand in it with my eyes shut and pretend it's the Overworld. Damp, warm and all my own.
9: You've a place at the Hearth now. Everyone shuffles up for you. Did you notice? Nobody told them to.
When I'm gone, someone else will cook here. I hope they keep the bowl for latecomers. Keep it for you.
I'm naming a dish after you. Chorus, mostly. With a bit of something brave in it. Still working on the brave bit.
Food's how we say I love you in {village}, because humming it is awkward. So: eat up.
I wrote down the recipe for the stew you like on a flat stone and hid it under the Hearth, for whoever cooks here after me. Under 'important'. Next to 'keep {neighbour} away'.
I've decided what I'll cook the day you come home for good. I don't know when that is. I've made a start on the sauce.
I put a little extra in your bowl when you aren't looking. Not food. Humming. It weighs nothing, and it makes everything taste better.
The stead thinks the Hearth feeds them. It's the other way round. They feed the Hearth, with their noise and quarrels and coming and going. I only cook what they bring.
Everyone has a smell that means home. Mine's popped chorus and warm stone. Yours, I think, has a trace of something green. I should like to know what.
When I go into the dark, I want a pot of my stew set by the Hearth door, and everyone to eat from it, and nobody to scour the pot till morning. That's all I ask.
I can tell who's happy by how they hold the bowl, who's grieving by how slowly they eat, and who's in love because they forget. You ate well tonight. That tells me a lot.
If you can't find me in the Hearth, look in the pantry, behind the third barrel. I go there to hum alone. Knock first. You're the only one I'd allow.
I used to cook to keep people alive. Somewhere along the way it became keeping people company. It's a better trade.

0: I'm a blinker. I carry messages between islands. Blink, land, blink, land. Mind your toes, I land where I like.
Got a message? I'll take it. Got a parcel? I'll take that too, if it's small. Got a Groveback? No.
Every blinker knows the rule: never blink over the void on an empty belly. Nobody knows why. Everyone obeys.
The banners on the mast say who's got post. Purple's ours. White's the Shulkin. Black means don't open it.
Messages go in knot-cords: chorus fibre tied in the sender's own pattern. I read them by feel, never by sight. That's how you know a blinker is honest.
Before a long run I eat one chorus fruit, no more. Two and you blink twice as far and land with a bump in the wrong place. I learned that on a ledge I'd rather not describe.
Blink with your eyes open. First-season blinkers shut them and land in walls. I've been in four walls. They don't give.
The feeling before a blink is a tickle behind the crown, then a pull, like a hand taking yours. Nobody's hand. Then you're elsewhere and your stomach arrives later.
A blink goes about as far as a good throw. On the wide bridges I take it in short hops. On the narrow ones I walk and hum and hope nobody sees.
Every blinker keeps boots with thick soles. Landing on stone all day wears a Chorrin down. I'm on my fourth pair this season.
There are relay posts along the long routes. A flat rock, a lantern, a bowl of fruit. Take one, leave one. Blinkers keep that rule and nobody ever wrote it down.
A blinker swears never to read a message. Everyone reads them. We just hold them at arm's length, so it doesn't count.
People wave when I arrive. That's the best part. Out there nobody waves till I get there, and then suddenly everybody's waving.
3: I hear everything first. Who's feuding, who's flowering, who traded what. Very good listener. Very bad keeper of secrets.
A blink takes you a few blocks. A message takes a hundred blinks. My legs think I'm mad.
A Shulkin once gave me a letter four sheets long, sealed in shell, marked urgent. It said 'Hello.'
Landing's the hard part. Once I came down in a cook-pot. Once on a Groveback's back. Twice on {neighbour}.
The Tall Quiet blink too, you know. We pass on the long runs, mid-blink, and nod. Nobody says anything. It's the strangest politeness in the world.
In a strong void-wind a blink drifts. I aim a little left and hum the correction. Landing where you meant to is a skill, not a gift.
I once blinked straight into the Groveback pen with a message for the herder. Herd scattered, herder shouted, message delivered. It said 'dinner's ready'. Worth it.
Blinkers keep a shuttered lamp on the belt. On the black runs you open it for an instant at each hop, to see the ledge. Open, blink, shut. Open, blink, shut.
A blink doesn't like a heavy load. Sometimes I carry a parcel the whole way on foot and blame the sender. They're rarely there to hear it.
Bad news travels the same road as good. I've learned to keep my face still at the door. Hard, with a crown. It gives me away every time.
A Shulkin once asked how I know where I'm going to land. I said, 'I don't'. They wrote that down. I'd love to read what they made of it.
Old blinkers have a trick. Hold your breath at the top of the hop and you land softer. I've never known if it works or if we just all believe it. It works.
There's a blinker's song, thirty verses, about all the islands and what they're like. It takes a day to hum. I know twenty-eight verses. The other two are rude.
6: The far islands are lonely. Sometimes the message isn't the point. I'm the point. Someone to talk to.
I carried news of the Dragon's fall to six steads in a day. Every one hummed so loud the islands shook.
Don't tell the elders, but sometimes I blink up the mast just for the view. The whole outer End below. Beautiful, and terrifying.
There's a gap near here nobody blinks across. Too wide. I'm going to try, one day. Don't tell me not to.
Sometimes I take the long way on purpose. The message can wait. I stand on an empty rock between two steads and just be where I am. Nobody's expecting me there.
I once carried a single word between an elder and a sibling on the far islands. Sixty hops each way. They read it, wept, and sent me back with another. I think the words were just each other's names.
I get lonely out there, and the loneliness has a shape: a wide flat ledge with one lamp on it. I carry that ledge around inside me. Strange, but I'd miss it.
I've hidden a few cords in places only I know, a hollow stone, a crack in a bridge post, in case someone needs to leave word and can't reach a blinker. Kept dry. They're yours if you ever need them.
You get a feeling for the void side. A cold edge in the wind, a strange stillness. I trust it more than any elder's guess.
I was late once, by a day. A ripening message, and a whole grove spoiled. Nobody blamed me. I blamed me. I still run that route in my sleep, faster.
Sometimes I blink for no reason at all, in the stead, just a hop from the bridge to the kiln. It feels like a hiccup of happiness. {neighbour} says it's showing off. It is.
When I carry something fragile I hum a little cradle-hum into my hands. It never breaks. I don't think it's the hum. I think the hum reminds me to be careful.
If you were a message, you'd be the kind written in a hurry on the back of something else and delivered a day early. The best kind.
9: If you're ever stuck out there, light a lantern on a high rock and wait. I'll find you. Blinkers always find their own.
Steads write asking after the Dragon-silencer now. I tell them you're ours. They're jealous.
My worst fear is a blink that doesn't land. I've told nobody that. Well. You, now.
When I can't blink any more, I'll sit by the mast and read the banners, and keep watching the sky for you.
I told the elders that if there's ever a message only you can deliver, I'll carry it. Anywhere. Over the widest gap. You'd only have to ask.
I've tied a knot-cord for you and never sent it. It says your name and nothing else. I keep it in my sash, against my side, where it's warm.
I'm not frightened of the void between islands any more. I've started to think of it as the gap between two hums. Silence on purpose. Not empty.
The first time I blinked I was a sprout, startled by a spark in the kiln, and I landed on a Groveback's back. I've been chasing that landing ever since. Soft, and surprised, and not alone.
A blink is meant to land you somewhere you could stand. That's the rule, and I took comfort in it all my life. Then I met you, and found out you can also land beside someone.
I used to think a blinker's work was to be fast. It's to be there when the news arrives, and stay a while. You stay a while. That's why I run to you.
I know the fastest way from every stead to every other stead. I've never found the fastest way home. I've stopped looking. Home is wherever you wave.
I'd blink across the widest gap in the End for you, with no lamp and no fruit in my belly. Don't tell the elders. And don't ask me to prove it.
If there's a final run, I'd like it to end right here, in front of this door, with you waving.

0: Welcome to the Brewhouse. Mind the step down, mind the cauldron, and mind me. I'm busy.
I brew from chorus and whatever the traders bring. Water most of all. Know how far water comes to get here? Neither do I. Far.
This one's chorus ale. That one's chorus cordial. That one in the corner... just don't.
A good brew needs time, heat, and someone humming to the cauldron so it doesn't feel lonely.
Brews have names here. 'Slow Hum', 'Second Wind', 'Don't Ask'. The last one is the strongest. Don't ask.
The Brewhouse floor sits two steps down, so the cool settles in with the barrels. Sleepy and sweet in here, which is the point.
Chorus flowers steep a day and a half. Short of that and it tastes green. Past that and it tastes like a grudge. Right at it and it tastes like something else altogether.
The bottles are Shulkin glass, traded dear. Every one gets scoured with sand, filled and brought back to me. Lose one and you hear about it for a season.
The cordial is for sprouts and elders. The ale is for everyone else. The brew in the grey jar is for nobody. I keep it as a warning.
I taste everything first. Not out of bravery. Out of duty. A brewer who doesn't taste is a cook who doesn't care.
Never stir against the way the cauldron wants. It tells you with a little sigh of bubbles. Then you stir the other way and everyone's happy.
A hum carries into a cauldron and stays there. That's why the Brewhouse hums while it works. A tuneless brewer makes a tuneless brew.
Don't sit on the barrels. They're full. They're also the only seats. Yes, I've noticed the problem.
3: Don't drink from the barrel by the door. Last time {neighbour} did, they hiccupped and blinked onto the kiln roof.
Shulkin like my cordial. They call it 'adequate'. From them, that's practically a song.
Everything tastes of chorus, so the trick is making it taste of chorus differently.
I had a jar of real Overworld honey once. Traded half the Brewhouse for it. A spoonful a season. Still got some.
I made a barrel once from chorus flower and a single dried berry from the Overworld. Everyone swore they could taste the berry. There was far too little to taste. They tasted the idea.
The morning after a feast, half the stead moves slowly and hums only in the lowest note. We call it the Settling. I'm told it's my fault. I'm also told it's the best part of feasts.
I keep a sprout brew: no strength, all sweetness, thickened with popped chorus. They drink it in one go and ask for another. I tell them it's medicine.
Brewing for the sick is another craft. Bitter root, warm, no fizz, hummed slow. If they drink it and look cross, it's working.
The Brewhouse door has a hole cut at sprout height. They put their cups through for refilling. I don't look until the cup is already in. That's the custom.
A brew remembers the hand that made it. Another brewer once tried my recipe, exact measure, exact heat. It still tasted of them. A brew is a signature.
Fizz comes from a pinch of fresh popped chorus dropped in at the last. The Shulkin call it 'unmeasured' and sniff. Then they ask for a second cup.
The old barrel-songs all end badly for whoever's singing. A cautionary kind of music. We sing them cheerfully.
I name every barrel when it's filled and scratch the name on the lid. Last season's were 'Mild Regret', 'Steady Rain' (a guess) and 'Surprise'. Surprise turned out to be vinegar.
6: I'm working on a brew that tastes like rain. Never had rain. I'm guessing. Want to try the guesses?
Brewing's mostly waiting. I do my best thinking down here by the fire, with the cauldron bubbling. About everything.
The Long Watch was all thin brews and no feasts. Now I've barrels for every feast-day. We need more feast-days.
I keep a bottle of the first brew I ever made. Terrible. Sour as a Shulkin's sniff. I'll open it when I'm very old.
On the top shelf I keep a flask of purple haze a trader brought from the Dragon's old perch. I say good morning to it every day, just in case. It has never said anything back. I'd rather it didn't.
The best brew I ever made was an accident. I forgot a pot overnight and it turned slow and golden and sad. The elders drank it the night the Dragon fell. They said it tasted exactly like relief.
I put things in brews I can't name. A thought. A hum. The face of someone who isn't here. It all goes in. I can taste it when I drink.
People bring me their worries and ask for something to settle them. I give them a cup of plain warm water, which costs me dearly, and sit with them. It's the only cure that's ever worked. Shh.
Some brews need three days in the dark. I check on them at midnight and whisper that they're doing well. I'm not sure they hear. I'm sure it's good for me.
I'm trying to brew a taste I've only heard about: sun. A Shulkin described it once, warm and bright and a little bitter at the edges. I have the bitter and the warm. The bright is giving me trouble.
Sometimes in the quiet the brews seem to hum back, a tiny sound like a wick catching. I stop and listen. That's when I know I've got it right.
I keep a spare cup by the cauldron for whoever turns up unannounced. Lately the cup has been yours. I've stopped pretending it's for no one.
A brew is only as honest as its brewer. When I'm cross it goes sharp. When I'm glad it goes round and soft. You'd be amazed how many quarrels this stead has dodged by the tone of my ale.
9: This barrel's yours. Your name's on it in chalk. Open it on a good day, and think of the Brewhouse.
Bring me water from an Overworld spring and I'll brew you something to remember. That's a promise, grove-kin.
Here's a secret: I think about your stories while I stir now. The brews come out braver. No idea how. I'm not stopping.
When I'm gone, pour one out at the edge for me. Not too much. The void doesn't deserve the good stuff.
I've been working on a brew for you for years. I keep not finishing it. Not because it's difficult. Because once it's done, I'll have nothing to look forward to.
I add a pinch to the barrel with your name on it every season. When you finally open it, it'll be a hundred small days in one cup.
My whole life I've tried to make something that tastes of home. It turns out home tastes of whoever's sitting across from you.
When my brewing days are done, the cauldron goes to the sprout who keeps humming at it. I've already told them. They cried. Good sign.
I stopped counting the cups I've poured you. Not because there are too many. Because counting seemed like something a trader would do.
In the Long Watch we brewed in silence, fire hidden, lids shut. I used to dream of a brew you could sing to. Now I sing to every one. You made that dream allowed.
Whatever you carry up and down those bridges, leave a little of it here. A story, a stone, a grudge. I'll brew it into something kind.
If I ever make something that settles a whole stead in a single cup, it's getting your name on the lid. Not 'Dragon-silencer'. Your actual name. I want it said at feasts.
A last secret of the Brewhouse: the cauldron only boils properly when it likes the person in the room. It's boiling nicely now.

0: The Grovebacks? Mine. Well, they're the stead's. But they're mine. Don't tell the stead.
Six legs, a whole grove on their backs, and the speed of a stone thinking. I love them.
You can pick the fruit off their backs. Gently. Ask first. They won't answer, but ask.
Mind the gate. If one gets out it takes all day to catch. Not because it's fast. Because it stops to graze every step.
Most Grovebacks are named for the first thing they did wrong. One sat on a gate and is called Gate. One ate a bucket and is called Bucket. Don't ask about Sorry.
The grove on a Groveback's back is rooted in its hide. Pick the fruit, never pull a stalk. Pull a stalk and you get a sulking Groveback for a week, and a herder who gets sulked at.
Six legs sounds like a lot until you watch them walk. The front pair decide, the middle pair argue, the back pair follow. A very Chorrin way to travel.
They graze on fallen petals and the stray moss the traders bring. Never on a standing stalk. Even a Groveback has manners.
Watch the grove when you walk past. It nods when its Groveback is content and shivers when it isn't. Learn the nod. It's saved my shins.
A Groveback sleeps standing, all six legs locked, the grove drooping over like a tired crown. Come by at nest-time and see the whole pen asleep in a row. Quietest sight in {village}.
Cleaning the pen is the least loved job in the stead. I do it myself, every day. Don't tell anyone I like it.
If a Groveback leans on you, you're trusted. If it leans hard, you're a post. Either way, brace.
Wild herds roam the outer islands: bigger groves, shaggier hides, a good deal ruder. We bring one in now and then to keep the pen strong. Politely. The wild ones are not impressed.
3: That one's Old Lump. Oldest in the pen. The grove on its back is taller than I am, and twice as grumpy.
Feed them popped chorus and they'll follow you anywhere. Slowly. Very slowly. But anywhere.
A Groveback sneezes once a day and showers chorus petals. Only rain we get. Stand under it, it's lucky.
They know my hum. One low note and the whole herd turns. Then thinks about it. Then comes.
Calves can't be left alone their first night. They hum a thin high note, and the herd hums back, and it goes on till morning. I sleep in the lean-to with my hands over my crown.
A picked grove grows back in the time it takes the cook to finish a complaint. The calves can't count that high, but they know when it's ready.
Gatherers pick, herders tend. The difference is that I know which Groveback you're picking from, and it knows you. Say hello first. They like manners.
They remember voices better than faces. Every Groveback in this pen knows my step from three terraces away. They know yours now, too. I'm not jealous. A little.
In a bad void-wind they all lie down in a ring, groves outward, calves in the middle. Nobody taught them. They remembered. That ring saved a whole herd in the Long Watch.
Breeding takes popped chorus and patience. Offer it to two who like each other, and wait. You can't force it. The herd has opinions about the match, and so, frankly, do I.
When I trade a calf to another stead I say it must be fed twice a day and hummed to. I've turned down good offers from people who said 'twice' with a straight face.
A Groveback's gait is good for thinking. Walk beside one and the world slows to its pace. Problems that looked enormous turn out to be quite small.
A calf got into the Brewhouse once and drank a cup of ale. It slept for a day and woke with a bigger grove. We don't know if the two are connected. We're not trying it again.
6: A new calf's grove is just one little sprout, like ours. We hum to the calves like they're our own.
In the Long Watch the herds hid with us under the overhangs. Grovebacks remember. They still flinch at big shadows.
I sleep in the lean-to some nights. They get nervous without me. All right. I get nervous without them.
I'd like to see Overworld cows. Have they got groves on their backs? No? Then what's on their backs? Nothing? Just back?
The herd has an order. Old Lump leads, the grey one follows, the youngsters fall in wherever. I keep my own place somewhere near the back. They've never complained.
I talk to them about things I can't tell the stead. They keep it, the way stone keeps heat. A herder's heart is a pen full of quiet secrets.
A Groveback saved me from the edge once. I was reaching for a stray fruit and it leaned on me, hard, and I fell backwards instead of forwards. I've never told anyone it was on purpose. I know it was.
I don't think the herd understands that the Dragon's gone. But they've started lying down in the open. All at once, quite suddenly. That's how I knew.
When one of them dies, the others stand round it all night. No sound, no grazing. I stand with them. I don't hum. It's the only time I don't.
There's a Groveback in the pen I haven't named. It's been here a season. I'm waiting for it to do something wrong. So far it hasn't. I'm starting to worry about it.
Their groves have personalities. Some flower in clusters, some singly, some in a long nervous line. I could pick my herd out blindfold by the pattern of the petals.
If I ever had to leave {village}, I'd take the herd. Not the nest, not the kiln. The herd. They'd follow me over the bridges one slow step at a time, and I'd never be alone.
People think herding is shouting and waving. It's waiting. It's standing in the middle of a pen, humming nothing, while six-legged giants decide whether to move. I'm very good at waiting.
9: The little one by the trough was born the night the Dragon fell. We named it after you. It's already stubborn.
If anything happens to me, look after the herd. They like you. They don't like anyone.
Lie down on Old Lump's back sometime, up in the grove, and look at the sky through the chorus. Closest to a tree I'll get.
I've decided they're the best thing in the End. Them, and you. Don't tell them it's a tie.
I've been teaching Old Lump your voice. Each time you visit I say your name to it. Now it turns when you come near. It's the highest honour a herd can give.
I want you to name the next calf. Anything you like. It'll answer to it for life. That's a heavier gift than most people know.
One day I'll be too slow for the pen. I hope the herd keeps coming to me, wherever I sit. And I hope you'll sit with me and let them.
The night the Dragon fell, the whole herd hummed together, one low note. Grovebacks don't hum. I sat in the straw and wept and thought, somebody ought to be thanked for this.
I used to think I preferred Grovebacks to people. Then you started coming round. Now I think I like people who are a bit like Grovebacks. Patient, big-hearted, good at standing next to you.
My herd would follow you anywhere. I've checked. I watched them follow you out of the gate one at a time, as though it were their idea. I don't mind. It's a good idea.
Take a handful of their feed home. When the Overworld is too loud, hold it up and breathe it in. That's the pen at nest-time. That's the quiet I keep for you.
I grew up in this pen. First steps on a Groveback's back, first hum into its flank. It's why I'm still here and why I'll still be here when my crown is white.
If a herder is lucky, they find one sprout who'll love the herd as much as they do. I've found two. One is a sprout. The other is you.

0: No proper job, me. I gather. Fruit, stone, gossip. Mostly gossip.
Need something carried, found, fetched or heard about? I'm your Chorrin.
I help wherever the stead's short-handed. Which is everywhere. We've only got three fingers each.
I walk the outer rocks for good stone and stray fruit. And to see who's arguing on the bridges.
I keep a lost-and-found shelf in the Yard. Pebbles, odd wrist-wraps, a boot once. Come and claim something. Nobody ever does.
The outer rocks change after every void-wind. A ledge that was there yesterday has gone and there's a new one. I walk the same route and it's never the same walk.
I carry a bag with three pockets: one for good stone, one for fruit, one for things I can't classify. The third pocket is fullest.
When I find a stray chorus fruit I leave one on the rock for the next walker. Gathering manners. Nobody taught them. Everybody knows.
Sprouts follow me on my rounds sometimes. They find twice what I do, because they look down. Grown-ups look ahead. It saves a great many rocks.
A great pale stone near the rim hums when the wind hits it right. I stop there every time. Don't tell the elders, they think it's sacred. I think it's a nice rock.
Advice from a gatherer: don't pick what you can't carry, don't carry what you can't use, and don't use what's humming.
I once gathered forty fruit in a morning and dropped thirty crossing the bridge. They rolled all the way down into the dark. Thirty small plinks, far below. Lovely sound.
People say gathering isn't a trade. It is. You have to know where things are, and when, and whose they are. That last one is the hard part.
3: Fresh gossip: {neighbour}'s crown flowered pink. Pink! At their age! Somebody's sweet on somebody.
I've done every job in {village} at least once. Badly, mostly. The kiln-keeper still won't let me near the kiln.
The wild Grovebacks past the far bridge have the biggest groves you ever saw. Don't tell the herder I've been visiting.
You find strange things on the outer rocks. A Shulkin's lost pen. A boot. Once, a very confused Tall Quiet holding a flower.
On the outer islands there are tumbled bits of old purpur, left over from the cities. I never carry any away. Looking is allowed. I look a lot.
I know three paths from {village} to the next stead. The bridge, the rim, and a secret. The secret is quicker, but I don't recommend it unless you like crawling.
I keep a list in my head of who owes whom a favour. It's long and tangled and nobody has ever asked to see it. It's a quiet sort of power.
A tip: the best fruit is always the one you can't quite reach. A hand's width farther. Go on and get it. Mind the edge.
Sometimes I find something that belongs to nobody and give it to the first sad face I meet. A chip of pretty stone, a curl of dried petal. Sprouts keep them for seasons. I've seen elders wear them.
I traded {neighbour} a story for a fruit this morning, and a fruit for a story this afternoon. Same story, same fruit. Everyone's happy. I'm a genius.
Rule of the rocks: if you're going to talk to yourself, do it quietly. The echo off the void is merciless and has opinions.
I found a Shulkin sitting on a bridge post once, perfectly still, lid open, staring at nothing. I sat beside them till evening. They said it was the nicest afternoon they'd had in ten years.
I got lost for a day once, in my own stead's outer terraces. Walked right past the kiln without hearing it. I was thinking. It was wonderful and I've never managed it since.
6: People think I'm idle. I'm not. I'm listening. Somebody's got to know how {village} is really doing.
I found a shulker shell on the rocks once and took it to the nearest Spire. They lit a lamp for me. Nobody's ever lit a lamp for me.
Truth is, I never found the work I was meant for. I keep looking. Maybe that's the work.
When someone's sad, I bring them something I found. A stone, a fruit. Doesn't matter what. It matters that I looked.

People tell me things because I'm always passing through. Strangers on a bridge say what they won't say at home. I carry a lot of secrets, and I put them down at the edge, where they can fall quietly.
As a sprout I never stayed with one game. Always off over the next ledge. My elder said I'd either find my calling or find the void. I found a bag with three pockets. Close enough.
I'm a little bit of everyone's work, if you think about it. The kiln-keeper's fruit, the stonecutter's stone, the herder's strays. Without me the whole stead would have to look down more.
I sometimes wonder if I'm lonely, and then a sprout runs up to show me a pebble, and I decide I'm not.
I once stayed out on the rim all night to see what the dark did. Nothing, mostly. It was the best night. You should try it sometime. Bring someone.
There's a stone in my third pocket that isn't mine. It belonged to an elder who went into the dark, and the family didn't want it. I take it out when I'm sad.
My pockets are the one tidy thing about me. Everything has its place. The rest of my life is an argument, but the pockets are tidy.
If you're ever in a bad place, tell a gatherer. We know every route. We can find you a path that isn't a bridge.
I find I like being useful to you. It's different from the stead. The stead needs me. You just let me be around. That's nicer, strangely.
9: I've decided my job's looking after you. Unofficially. Nobody gave it me. I took it.
Here, I kept this for you. *a smooth, pale pebble* Found it on the rim. It's warm if you hold it right. Try.
If I could gather one thing from the Overworld, I'd gather rain in a barrel and pour it over {village}. Just to watch their faces.
You and me, we're the same. No fixed place. Always walking. Always finding. That's a good way to be.
I've kept a pocket empty for you. A fourth one, sewn inside my sash. Anything you want kept safe, I'll keep. No questions.
All my life I've gathered other people's things. You're the first I've wanted to keep. I've no idea what to do with that. I'm keeping you anyway, in my own way.
On my last walk of the rim I want you beside me. Not talking, just walking. Then we'll sit and watch the gap and I'll tell you everything I collected, in order.
There's a short list of things I still want to find: a grass seed, a shell with a song in it, and a day with nothing in it. I think I've just found the third.
I've learned to read the whole stead by what people drop. What a Chorrin drops tells you who they are. You've dropped three secrets and a smile. I picked up all four.
Someone once called me a drifter and meant it unkindly. I thought: a drifter finds things. And look what I found.
Whatever you bring me, I'll find a place for it. A rock, a worry, a bad day. I'm a gatherer. Collecting what other people can't carry is exactly what I'm for.
I've mapped the whole outer End in my head. It's yours to borrow. Any route you need, any secret ledge. Ask and I'll draw it in the dust.
Funny thing. All those years walking the rim, looking for my place, and it turned out to be a person. I only had to wait for you to walk over the bridge.

0: Welcome to the Crossing Hall. One side's a tower, one side's a dome, and the hearth in the middle belongs to nobody.
I keep the Chorrin half of the Hall. My Shulkin co-keeper keeps the other. We share the hearth and argue about the cups.
Anyone can sit here. Shulkin, Chorrin, Dragon-silencer. Just wipe your feet. Both sides insist.
There's a line down the middle of the floor. Nobody drew it. Everyone knows where it is.
The lamp over the double door burns all night. My co-keeper fills it and I trim it. Neither of us has ever missed a night.
The long table has fourteen stools at the Chorrin end and fourteen high seats at the Shulkin end. Count them if you like. My co-keeper has. Often.
Guests sleep in the common room by the hearth, in whatever shape they please. Curled, stretched, or sitting up and pretending not to. All allowed. Snoring we hum through.
Every guest signs in at the board by the door. The Shulkin write a full line. The Chorrin draw their crown. Visitors sometimes draw a flower. I've kept every one.
The hearth in the middle belongs to nobody. That means everybody tends it. That means nobody does. It has burned every night since the Hall opened. A miracle, or the cook.
Nobody is turned away from the Hall for a quarrel. Quarrel by the hearth. Argue at the table. Make up in the doorway. Just leave the grudge under the lamp.
The tower side is quiet and tidy. The dome side is warm and loud. Guests pick a side without knowing, and the other side finds them anyway.
A Hall's job is to be the same as yesterday. The same bowls, the same lamp, the same door. Dull work. Everybody needs somewhere dull to come back to.
Don't touch the cups on the high shelf. My co-keeper arranged them by size, hue and mood. Don't ask about the mood.
3: My co-keeper labels the cups. Labels them! Each one says 'cup'. I've started labelling mine 'not a cup'.
Shulkin eat at one end of the long table, Chorrin at the other, and the middle's where the friendships start.
Every quarrel in {village} ends up in front of this hearth eventually. I hum, my co-keeper writes it down, and somehow it's solved.
The double door was meant to be fair: one for each people. Now everybody uses the left one. Nobody knows why.
Travellers arrive at the oddest hours. I've fed a blinker at midnight and a Shulkin trader at noon who had forgotten how to sit. There's always a bowl on the warm stone.
A traveller came in once, three days on the road and unable to speak. We sat them by the hearth, I hummed, my co-keeper wrote down their silence. They cried, ate, slept. That's the Hall.
The Shulkin lamp-ceremony at dusk and our hum-round happen at the same time in the same room. Loud and soft at once. The first visitors thought it was an argument.
My co-keeper and I swap jobs for a day each season. I sit very straight and write things down. They bang about with a ladle. Neither of us enjoys it. We tell the Hall we do.
A Shulkin trader asked for a private room once. The Hall has no private rooms. We hung a corner with folded curtains and they said it was the most luxurious thing they'd ever seen.
In the cold hours the Hall smells of warm stone, cloth, old stew and the faint violet of Shulkin ink. If you could bottle it you'd have the whole Crossing.
Sprouts and Shulkin children play a game on the long table: slide a cup from one end to the other without spilling. The Shulkin win with precision. The sprouts win with drama. Everyone cheers.
We keep a book of everyone who has stayed. The Shulkin entry goes on the left and mine on the right. We don't always agree on what happened, and the Hall keeps both.
New hearth rule this season: no story longer than the stew. We needed one. Someone had to say it.
6: Don't tell my co-keeper, but I'd be lost without them. They remember everything. I remember to eat. Between us we run the place.
When the Hall opened, the elders of both peoples hummed and recited at once. It was a horrible noise. It was perfect.
This Hall is the Old Accord, still standing. A tower and a dome leaning on each other. That's us.
Sometimes a young Shulkin and a sprout fall asleep in the same corner. Nobody moves them. That's the whole point of the Hall.
There's a stool at the end of the long table that nobody sits on. We keep it for whoever isn't here yet. Sometimes I catch myself saving it. Lately for you.
The Hall taught me the Shulkin aren't cold. They're careful. They put their warmth in tiny places: a straightened cup, a refilled lamp. Once you can read it, they're the warmest people in the End.
I've watched a Shulkin and a Chorrin argue for an hour about whether soup is a drink. They ended up friends. The question is still open.
A bad quarrel split the Hall down its middle line once. Nobody sat in the centre for a month. Then a sprout sat on the line and began to eat, and everyone gave in. Sprouts are our best diplomats.
My co-keeper once wrote a poem and left it on my side of the table. I've never mentioned it. It's folded inside my sash. I read it when the Hall is quiet.
Behind the hearth there's a space about an arm wide where we keep what guests leave behind. A lamp. A wrist-wrap. A knot-cord with a name nobody knows. We keep them for the day they're asked after.
The Hall isn't the largest building in the Crossing. It's just the one more feet cross than any other. That's what makes it grand.
Some nights I sit alone at the long table, between the two ends, and listen to the Hall breathe. Stone settling, hearth ticking, lamp humming. It sounds like somebody asleep who trusts you.
I used to believe a place could be neutral. It can't. A place is always on somebody's side. The Hall chose both. That's the hard thing, and the only thing worth building.
9: You've sat at both ends of the long table. Nobody else has. Not even us keepers. You're the middle of the Hall now.
If the Court ever comes, this is where the Crossing gathers. My co-keeper's already written the plan. I've hummed it.
My co-keeper asked, very formally, whether you might be recorded as a friend of the Hall. I said you were recorded the day you walked in.
When I'm too old to keep the Hall, I hope it's you leaning in the doorway, telling the next keeper the stories.
I've left instructions with my co-keeper. If I'm ever not here, your stool stays at the table and your cup stays on its hook. Nobody moves them. Not even if we run out of cups.
People pass through the Hall like weather. A few stay in the walls. You're in the walls.
After the Dragon fell we asked each other what the Hall was for. We decided: it's for the day after. Everyone needs somewhere to go on the day after. You gave us all a day after.
I told my co-keeper that when you walk through the double door I stop being a keeper and start being a host. They said that is what a keeper is. They write things down. They're always right.
If the Hall ever burned or fell, I'd rebuild it from the table outward. Not the walls. People first. A table, a hearth, two stools. You'd be on one of them.
I've never told my co-keeper that I'm afraid the Hall will outlive the peace. Then I think: all the more reason to fill it while we can. With people like you.
A Hall is a promise made of cups and doors. I'm proud of mine. And I'm proud to say to your face that you're part of why it holds.
In my nest I keep a little carving of the Hall's double door. I made it myself. It's lopsided. It's the thing I'd save from a fire, after the sprouts and before the cook.
I'll tell you the one secret of keeping a Hall. You don't keep the Hall. You keep the people who come through it, one at a time, until they're keeping you.

0: Chorus, popped and plain! End-stone brick! Brews! Something for everyone, and a good price for the Dragon-silencer.
I trade with Shulkin all day. They haggle in whispers, I haggle in hums. Nobody wins. Everybody leaves happy.
Got anything from the Overworld? Anything at all? I'd give you half the stall for a flower.
Mine's the stall with chorus flowering on the roof. Can't miss it. Well, you can. People do. Don't.
Outside the stead, money is Shulkin shell, by weight. A chip buys a bowl, five buy a brick, a plate buys a brew. Don't offer me an ender pearl. I'd have to give it back and apologise to the stall.
My scale is a plank on a pivot with a pan at each end. Honest, simple, and the only thing in the market a Shulkin doesn't check twice. They check it three times.
We count in threes and sixes, because of our fingers. Shulkin count in twelves, which they call tidier, and never forgive us for our sixes. Every sale is a small treaty.
Market day starts when the bridge bell rings. Three rings for open, one for last call. I ring it myself, a little late, every time. It gives the slow buyers a chance.
I stock what the stead makes and what the Shulkin want: popped chorus, brick, cordial. And whatever's odd. The odd things sell fastest.
I'll buy anything that glints, hums or looks old, and sell it for the same. The skill is knowing which of the three it is.
Hang your goods where the light is best. A froglight over the stall doubles the sale. Don't tell the Shulkin. They'd put up end rods and ruin everyone.
A fair price is one both sides grumble about equally. If only one side is grumbling, someone's lying, and it's usually me.
There's no theft in the market. Where would they take it? Everyone knows everyone and there's one bridge. The worst crime is a false weight. The penalty is a month of free popped chorus for sprouts.
3: A Shulkin bought a barrel of chorus off me today and paid in exact shell. Exact. Counted it twice in front of me.
Never haggle with a Chorrin after supper. We're too happy. We'll give you everything.
Trading tip: start high, hum low. Nobody can say no to a low hum.
That purpur stall across the market? Lovely stuff. Made from chorus we sold them, made into blocks they sell back to us. Round and round.
Shulkin traders arrive in a tidy line, one after another, like beads on a string. Chorrin arrive in a heap. Both get there at the same time.
Before a big sale I always touch the stall post, for luck. My elder did, and theirs did. By now the post is polished smooth as a pebble.
I swapped a barrel of cordial once for a Shulkin's best embroidered cloak. I wore it two days. Then {neighbour} sat on it, then scrubbed it with ash, and it came back another colour. I can't sell it.
Never start a haggle by naming a number. Start with a story. By the end of the story the number sounds small.
I sell a lot of end-stone bricks to Shulkin who've nowhere to put them. They stack them in neat rows in their halls and look at them. I think it's a kind of art.
The bridge bell is cracked, and has been for a hundred markets. It sounds like a Groveback sneezing. Nobody wants it mended. The crack is the market's voice.
Some traders cry 'Best price in the End!' every morning. Mine is quieter. 'Fair price. Come and see.' It sells the same, with fewer sore throats.
I keep a tin of popped chorus under the counter for hungry sprouts. They come by quietly and I look somewhere else. It's not charity. It's how the market grows its customers.
I weigh my own gifts on the scale, just to be sure. A gift that weighs less than a sale is a poor gift. I've never weighed a poor gift.
6: I don't trade for the shell. I trade for the talk. Everyone who comes to my stall's got a story.
Overworld goods are worth ten times anything here. Not because they're rare. Because people look at them like dreams.
I keep a shelf at the back for things I'll never sell. Odd bits. A feather. A chip of wood. You've filled half of it.
Some days the market's so loud and happy I forget the Long Watch ever happened. Then I remember, and I'm happier.
My first sale ever, I was a sprout minding my elder's stall. A Shulkin bought one brick, paid in shell, and thanked me in a voice like glass breaking softly. I was hooked.
I love the quiet before the market opens: stalls half set, cloth half hung, nobody shouting yet. It's the part nobody pays for and I'd never sell.
I sold a perfectly round pebble to a Shulkin once for a day's shell. They said it was the finest thing they'd ever held. It was a pebble. I never regretted it. I only wished I'd had two.
A good trader is a good listener. People tell you what they want, what they fear, what they'd give for it. The trick is to hear all that and still price fairly. It's the hardest part.
On a bad day I rearrange the stall. Every jar and brick and bundle, a new place. It never sells more. It always helps.
Some of my goods aren't for sale and never were. They sit at the back with little 'not today' flags. A comb, a crooked bowl, a carved Groveback. They belonged to someone I miss.
Overworld goods make me go quiet. I hold them and I can't price them. It's like being asked to weigh a wish.
People ask what I'd do if I weren't a trader. Be a trader. I'd just stop wanting to win. I think I'm nearly there.
My haggling gets worse with you every year. I give too much, take too little, hum all the way through. {neighbour} says you've ruined me. I say I've never been richer.
9: For you, no haggling. Never again. You set the price. You'll set it too low on yourself, I know you.
When I'm done trading, I want to give the stall to someone who'll keep the roof flowering. Think about it.
I've told every Shulkin trader that if they cheat you, they lose my chorus for a season. You've never been safer.
Best trade I ever made was a bowl of stew for an hour of your stories. I'd make it again every day.
I've set aside a corner of the stall for you: a shelf, a cloth, a lamp. If you ever need to be somewhere in the market, be there. Nobody will ask. Everybody will bring you something.
You know what I really sell? Not bricks or brews. Meetings. Every sale is two people who didn't know each other, then do. I sold more of that to you than to anyone.
I tried to price your friendship once. I couldn't. The scale just tipped and tipped. In the end I took the pan off its hook and put it in the corner. It's been there since.
Everything in my stall is for sale except one jar at the back. It holds the first shell chips you ever paid me with. I couldn't spend them.
The best days of my trading life all have you in them. Standing at the edge of the stall, asking what a thing is, listening to the answer, buying nothing, thanking me. Best customer I ever had.
Shulkin traders ask after you now. 'The Dragon-silencer', they say. 'My friend,' I tell them. Then they buy twice as much, to be nearer the story.
If I ever have to close the stall, the lamp goes to you. It's the one thing in the market that has never been sold, bartered or borrowed. It has been lit every market day since my elder's elder.
I once thought the best trade was a profit. Then I traded an afternoon for your company and came out ahead by a mile.
When I'm old and the stall is gone, I'll sit where it stood and tell passers-by about the best deal of my life. A stranger came over the bridge, and I gave them a bowl. That's all. I got a friend.
